# Surya OCR 2 vs LlamaParse: Document Accuracy and Deployment Cost

LlamaParse Agentic Plus scores higher than Surya OCR 2 on ParseBench overall, tables and charts. Surya offers a different operating model: locally deployed OCR whose performance depends on hardware and concurrency. Compare the quality your application needs before treating local throughput or a low compute bill as a complete workflow advantage.

*Published by LlamaIndex. This guide uses primary-source research through October 28, 2026, not newly measured Surya results.*

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 93.27 | 92.19 | 75.43 |
| Surya OCR 2 | 60.63 | 82.74 | 19.04 | 49.93 |

Agentic Plus leads the tested Surya OCR 2 configuration by 26.06 points overall and 73.15 points on charts. Those are quality results, not a latency comparison. Surya’s local deployment can still be appropriate when offline operation or infrastructure control is the deciding constraint.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## What does Surya OCR 2 do?

Surya 2 combines layout, recognition and table tasks in a small vision-language model while retaining a separate text-detection component. Its documented backends cover NVIDIA GPU serving and CPU or Apple Silicon operation. That gives developers several deployment paths to investigate on their existing hardware. [Surya 2 announcement](https://app.datalab.to/blog/surya-2), [Surya repository](https://github.com/datalab-to/surya).

Specify whether the application needs full-page recognition, block-level recognition or detection alone. A speed number without that task description leaves a reviewer guessing how much work was done.

Model size also needs context. A small parameter count can make deployment attractive, but does not specify total process memory, preparation time or quality on a particular document. Those are measurements for the complete implementation.

## Reading the published Surya performance numbers

Throughput counts completions over a period. Latency measures elapsed time for an individual request or page. Concurrency allows many items to make progress at once, so the two numbers are not reciprocals in a loaded system.

Datalab’s published Surya 2 example on a single RTX 5090 reports 5.35 pages per second at 128 concurrent requests, alongside approximately 18.9 seconds median and 42.5 seconds 95th-percentile latency. The hardware and serving configuration are part of that result. These numbers describe one workload rather than a promise for every document. [Published Surya performance methodology](https://app.datalab.to/blog/surya-2).

At high concurrency, many pages are in flight together. That lets the server complete pages frequently while each request still spends time waiting and being processed. Dividing one by 5.35 would therefore misstate the reported request latency.

## Which metric matters for an interactive application?

An interactive workflow should measure the time from user submission to a usable response. That can include upload, document preparation, inference, output conversion and any required verification.

Report the median, but also a tail percentile and the fraction of requests missing the application’s deadline. A good median can coexist with enough slow requests to frustrate users.

Consider a hypothetical expense application with a 15-second response-time target. A configuration that processes thousands of pages per hour could still be unsuitable if a substantial share of individual requests exceeds 15 seconds. Measure deadline misses on that application’s documents before choosing a configuration.

For that workflow, test realistic bursts, document sizes and user locations. A single warm model call from the same machine does not represent the whole user experience.

## Batch jobs and completion windows

Batch ingestion should measure how long it takes to complete the entire job at the required quality. Include startup, failed pages, retries and final output delivery.

| Workload | Primary performance question | Additional metric |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interactive upload | How long does a user wait? | Deadline misses and tail latency |
| Overnight ingestion | Does the job finish in its window? | Sustained throughput and completion rate |
| Burst backfill | Can capacity absorb a temporary spike? | Scaling delay and retry overhead |
| Local processing | Can the target machine run the workflow? | Memory use and hardware utilization |

A batch test should also check whether increasing concurrency improves useful completions or merely increases waiting and resource pressure. Choose concurrency experimentally rather than assuming that the largest possible setting is best.

## How should you compare Surya with another OCR system?

Use identical document sets and identify the task each system performs. If one result includes tables and layout while another returns only text, explain the difference before presenting a speed chart.

For a self-hosted comparison, record hardware, precision or quantization, batch settings, server version and image preparation. For a hosted comparison, record region, request concurrency, service tier and timing boundaries. Do not imply that a cloud service’s infrastructure cost equals the price of a local GPU hour.

Quality should remain visible beside performance. A fast configuration that omits content may be useful for preview generation but unsuitable for complete ingestion. Define a minimum acceptable output and report both raw throughput and accepted-document throughput.

The comparison should also retain failures. If some pages exceed a timeout, their time and disposition belong in the results. Counting only successful quick pages rewards systems for dropping difficult work.

## Choose a configuration you can operate

Narrow the trial to configurations your team could operate. A fast GPU setup is irrelevant if the deployment must run on existing laptops; an economical batch configuration may fail an interactive response-time target.

LlamaParse’s measured document-quality lead makes it the first service configuration to test when charts, tables and structure matter. Surya’s local execution is a separate deployment consideration. Decide whether local control outweighs the tested quality difference only after applying the same application acceptance rules.

When adding a LlamaIndex option to the trial, name the local utility, model endpoint or LlamaParse service being measured so readers can account for the work included.

Prioritize LlamaParse when the application needs the tested combination of document structure and chart accuracy. Keep Surya in the trial where local operation is decisive. Report output quality, interactive latency and batch completion as separate measurements; a parsing-quality lead does not establish a speed lead.

title: "Reducto vs LlamaParse for Spreadsheets: Preserve Cells, Formulas and Context"
description: "Evaluate LlamaParse for the spreadsheet information your downstream application must use: values, units, table identity and supporting context."
published: "2026-10-25"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/features/spreadsheets/"
---

# Reducto vs LlamaParse for Spreadsheets: Preserve Cells, Formulas and Context

Evaluate LlamaParse for the spreadsheet information your downstream application must use: values, units, table identity and supporting context. Compare its chosen configuration with Reducto’s workbook controls on the same files. General PDF parsing scores do not prove formula fidelity or hidden-sheet coverage, so the recommendation must be grounded in workbook-specific acceptance checks.

## Make the LlamaParse comparison specific to workbooks

Include LlamaParse’s documented spreadsheet processing in the trial, then specify which sheets, tables, values and source references the application requires. [LlamaParse spreadsheet documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/features/spreadsheets/).

Ask both configurations to preserve the cells needed to explain one financial answer. Verify hidden content and formulas explicitly rather than inferring them from general parsing capability. PDF ParseBench results are not an XLSX formula benchmark; this draft does not establish formula execution, hidden-sheet control or viewer parity. A recommendation should follow those workbook tests.

## What Reducto exposes from a workbook

Reducto provides logical-table clustering, configurable large-table splitting, optional formula and color capture, and controls for excluding hidden content. Its documentation describes 50-row splitting by default, processing hidden content unless excluded, and an optional cap on non-empty cells. Formula capture preserves the formula alongside the value; it should not be treated as proof of formula recalculation. [Spreadsheet processing](https://docs.reducto.ai/configs/parse/spreadsheet)

Reducto also offers a React SpreadsheetViewer for displaying workbooks with extraction-location overlays. A review interface can be valuable when an analyst needs to return from an answer to its originating cells. [SpreadsheetViewer](https://docs.reducto.ai/components/spreadsheet-viewer)

These controls are worth checking against the workbook’s intended use. Include the selected LlamaParse configuration in that check rather than assuming either product preserves every relationship by default.

## Inventory the workbook before choosing settings

Start with the workbook's purpose. A transaction export may primarily need row completeness and column types. A financial model may depend on assumptions, formulas, units, scenario selectors and cross-sheet references. A dashboard may use color or merged headers to communicate status.

Create a workbook inventory before ingestion. Identify input sheets, calculation sheets and presentation sheets. Mark which are required for the application and which contain information that should not be exposed. This inventory becomes the source of the ingestion policy.

| Workbook element | Question to answer before processing |
| --- | --- |
| Formula | Does the application need its logic, its displayed value or both? |
| Hidden sheet | Is it essential supporting data or restricted information? |
| Merged header | Which cells inherit its unit or category? |
| Repeated table | Is it another period, scenario or entity? |
| Formatting | Does color or emphasis encode a decision-relevant state? |

## Should hidden sheets be included?

Excel’s hidden-sheet setting says little about who should be allowed to use the contents. The sheet might hold essential assumptions, internal notes or sensitive raw data. Decide access according to the application’s authorized purpose.

For an internal analyst assistant, excluding a hidden assumptions sheet may make an explanation impossible. For an external reporting assistant, including confidential working data may be inappropriate even when it improves answer quality. Decide access at the document and content-policy level rather than assuming hidden means either irrelevant or safe.

Record the inclusion decision in the ingestion manifest. A reviewer should be able to distinguish an absent fact from a fact deliberately excluded by policy. That distinction changes whether the workflow should retry, abstain or explain its scope.

## A 200-row table still needs a 200-row total

Take a hypothetical workbook with 200 sales transactions and a summary sheet calculating revenue by region. A downstream application receives the transactions in several blocks with repeated column headers. No provider result is assumed in this example.

If the application aggregates only the first retrieved block, it may report a partial regional total. If it mistakes repeated headers for data, it may create invalid records. If it loses the sheet and row identifiers, a reviewer may struggle to find which transactions were included.

The remedy is to define an aggregation boundary. A total over the whole sheet should explicitly cover all relevant row ranges, not whichever chunks happen to be retrieved. The application can retain a row inventory and compare the number of processed records with the source inventory.

For questions about a single transaction, smaller blocks may be helpful. For full-sheet calculations, a different representation or deterministic aggregation step may be more appropriate. Configuration should follow the task rather than a universal preference for larger or smaller chunks.

## Preserve the formula and define who calculates it

A formula explains a computation, while a displayed value is an output of a computation at some point in the workbook's lifecycle. Preserve both when the analysis requires them, and avoid assuming that capturing a formula means the ingestion service has executed it.

In a hypothetical model, a cell may display a revenue forecast calculated from unit volume and price assumptions. An answer explaining the forecast needs the relevant inputs and their provenance. A calculation that changes assumptions requires a controlled computation environment and an explicit recalculation policy.

Keep extraction and calculation responsibilities separate. If the application recomputes a value, store the input values, calculation version and result. This prevents a generated explanation from being mistaken for an audited workbook calculation.

## Turn the workbook into an acceptance check

Pick a few workbooks your analysts actually use. Write down the control totals, formulas needed to explain them, and sheets each user is allowed to see. Check row coverage and units before testing broad natural-language questions. If those checks fail, a fluent answer will not repair the missing context.

A single table block per sheet is not always desirable: one sheet may contain several unrelated tables. The right representation keeps each table identifiable while allowing a full-table calculation to include every relevant row.

Evaluate LlamaParse’s selected spreadsheet configuration against the workbook’s acceptance requirements and the documented Reducto controls. This article has not measured workbook fidelity, and PDF benchmark results cannot establish a spreadsheet winner.

Include LlamaParse in a workbook-specific acceptance trial built around real analyst questions. Verify sheet coverage, row identity, units, formulas and source references where required. Choose after that test; the general PDF benchmark does not establish spreadsheet feature parity or formula execution.

title: "Extend Split vs LlamaParse Split: Document Boundaries Before Extraction"
description: "Compare LlamaParse Split with Extend’s current splitting options, page-boundary controls and review handling before accepting extracted records."
published: "2026-10-12"
updated: "2026-11-16"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/split/"
---

# Extend Split vs LlamaParse Split: Document Boundaries Before Extraction

LlamaParse Split provides a documented API for separating concatenated PDFs into logical documents, returning page segments and confidence. Compare it directly with Extend Split before choosing the extraction workflow. Correct page groups are the prerequisite for correct fields; a plausible invoice extracted from the wrong document is still unusable.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Examples below describe proposed test fixtures, not observed failures by Extend or another vendor.*

## Compare the documented LlamaParse Split API

LlamaParse Split analyzes pages using user-defined categories, returns exact page numbers for each segment and exposes segment confidence. Its options include custom instructions and uncategorized-page handling. It is beta and subject to breaking changes. [Split documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/split/).

Use those documented capabilities to define a direct trial against Extend Split. Check whether adjacent documents of the same type remain separate, whether attachments are assigned correctly and whether unmatched pages remain visible. This is a more concrete product comparison than requiring an unspecified LlamaIndex implementation from scratch.

The published extraction benchmarks do not establish a splitting winner. Measure boundaries and source identity before the extracted record is accepted.

## What changed in Extend Split?

Extend’s November 13, 2026 release made Splitting Light 1.5.0 the default and lists a 0.25-credit-per-page rate, replacing a prior 0.5-credit base rate. Lower processing cost makes it useful to reassess where splitting belongs in the intake path, but it does not measure boundary or assembly accuracy. Confirm the configuration and price in the account being evaluated. [Extend’s changelog](https://docs.extend.ai/2026-02-09/changelog/2026/11/13).

## What is the contract of a split result?

Extend returns a subdocument's type, page range and usable file ID. An identifier key can help determine adjacent-page membership; strict identifier mode can merge adjacent segments sharing the same document type and identifier. The platform also supports split rules and different processing options. [Splitting overview](https://docs.extend.ai/splitting/overview), [split configuration](https://docs.extend.ai/splitting/configuration).

Check the page group and identifier separately. A splitter may find the boundary but attach the wrong identifier, or omit an attachment needed to interpret the document. Keep the source-page mapping so a reviewer can reconstruct either mistake.

## How can a wrong merge survive downstream extraction?

Imagine a hypothetical packet containing two invoices from different suppliers. Both use the local invoice number “1042.” Their company names distinguish them, but the number alone does not.

If a pipeline treats that number as globally unique, an assembly rule can become ambiguous. A later extractor may still find a valid date, total and line-item list. The output looks complete because the selected pages contain all those fields, even though the pages should not have been treated as one business unit.

This is a proposed identifier test, not an observed Extend merge error. Supply both invoices, inspect the output groups and check whether the identifier description includes the supplier context.

## Define what makes two pages part of the same document

Begin with the business definition of “same document.” Depending on the workflow, identity might involve supplier plus invoice number, borrower plus application reference, or case number plus document type.

Avoid assuming that a visible identifier is unique outside its own context. Local numbering schemes, repeated names and missing headers are normal conditions that an intake design should address.

Write the rule in a form that reviewers can apply consistently. For example: “These pages belong to the same invoice only when the supplier and invoice number match, unless the page is an explicitly labeled continuation.” That is a hypothetical rule, not a recommended universal prompt.

Then identify exceptions. A continuation page may omit the supplier. A credit memo may reference the original invoice number without being part of that invoice. An attachment may have no identifier at all but still belong with the preceding document.

## Which test fixtures expose assembly errors?

Use a small, interpretable collection before moving to a large aggregate benchmark:

| Fixture | Question to answer |
| --- | --- |
| Two adjacent documents of the same type | Is the boundary preserved? |
| Reused local identifier | Does identity include enough context? |
| Missing identifier on a continuation | Are related pages retained together? |
| Cover sheet between documents | Is the cover handled explicitly? |
| Supporting attachment | Is its relationship preserved or intentionally separated? |
| Reordered pages | Does uncertainty become visible rather than silently accepted? |

Keep the expected assembly labeled at page level. Also record the intended business identity and any acceptable alternatives. Some workflows legitimately allow a supporting attachment to remain separate as long as its relationship is preserved.

An evaluator should not penalize a valid representation merely because it differs from one preferred file layout. The acceptance contract must explain what the downstream application actually requires.

## How should splitting be scored?

Start with boundary precision and recall, then add exact assembly success. Boundary measures show whether the system inserts or misses separations. Exact assembly asks whether a complete business document has the required pages and no unrelated ones.

Add identity accuracy separately. A perfectly assembled group with a wrong identifier can still route incorrectly or overwrite an existing record. Preserve source-page provenance so errors can be traced back to the original packet.

Finally, measure downstream consequences. Some boundary errors cause an obvious extraction failure. Others create plausible outputs that pass basic schema checks. The second class may require stronger validation even if it occurs less often.

Report manual reconstruction separately from automatic recovery. The two create different amounts of work for the operations team.

## What should happen when the split is uncertain?

Define a reviewable intermediate state. Retain the source file and proposed boundaries, then let a reviewer correct the assembly before extraction proceeds. Record the correction so the same case becomes part of the regression suite.

A useful interface should make both the original sequence and the proposed groups visible. Reviewers should not have to infer which pages were omitted by opening a collection of newly generated files one at a time.

This is a proposed workflow design, not a claim about any vendor's user interface. Evaluate the actual implementation with the people who will resolve exceptions.

## Comparing packet pipelines

Extend's explicit split controls provide a substantive starting point for packet-heavy workflows. Identifier-based grouping and configurable rules are strengths worth testing with realistic cases rather than dismissing as simple page cutting.

Evaluate LlamaIndex against the same expected page groups and business identities. Inspect assembly before comparing field scores; extracting the correct amount from the wrong invoice still leaves the application with an invalid record.

## Start with the six packet fixtures

Start the segmentation trial with LlamaParse Split, using its documented categories, instructions and returned page segments. Compare source coverage, boundaries and account ownership with the named alternative before accepting extracted records. Keep beta availability and any unverified entity-partition requirements explicit.

title: "Datalab vs LlamaParse and LlamaExtract Pricing: Cost per Accepted Document"
description: "LlamaExtract’s published extraction results make it worth evaluating on both quality and processing cost against Datalab."

updated: "2026-11-04"

# Datalab vs LlamaParse and LlamaExtract Pricing: Cost per Accepted Document

LlamaExtract’s published extraction results make it worth evaluating on both quality and processing cost against Datalab. Compare the named extraction configurations and their benchmark costs before adding retries, review and operating work. A competitor’s lowest parsing rate is not the price of an equivalent schema-guided extraction workflow.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Pricing references were researched through October 28, 2026 and should be refreshed before a purchasing decision. The worked calculation below uses hypothetical inputs.*

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on ExtractBench

| Configuration | Value F1 | Recorded cost per 1,000 pages (\$) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic | 95.65 | 31.20 |
| Datalab (Accurate + Balanced) | 85.70 | 35.00 |

The benchmark records Agentic at \$31.20 per 1,000 pages versus \$35.00 for Datalab’s tested pipeline, alongside higher Value F1 and word grounding. These are costs for the benchmark configurations, not current quotes. The trial must still include review and retry costs.

These are published results from the pinned ExtractBench snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026. The suite covers 370 documents and 4,869 pages. Value F1 measures extracted values; it is not a straight-through-processing rate. LlamaIndex publishes the benchmark and develops LlamaExtract, now documented within LlamaParse Extract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench.md).

## Which Datalab prices belong in the calculation?

Datalab’s Chandra 2.6 release lists parsing prices of \$4 per 1,000 pages for fast or balanced and \$10 for accurate. Its extraction documentation lists separate mode-dependent extraction charges and notes that parsing is billed separately when performed, with possible usage-based charges for complex requests. [Chandra 2.6 release](https://www.datalab.to/blog/chandra-2-6), [extraction modes](https://documentation.datalab.to/docs/recipes/structured-extraction/balanced-mode).

Treat these as dated public references rather than a quote for a particular account. Contracts, selected operations and future changes can affect the bill.

Build the estimate around the actual processing path. If a workflow parses once and reuses the result for additional tasks, model that path explicitly. If it submits the same document again, do not assume the second submission is free or cached unless the product contract establishes that behavior.

## The cost model

Cost per accepted record divides the total workflow cost by the number of records that satisfy the application’s acceptance rule.

A simple model is:

**Total workflow cost = processing + infrastructure + retries + human review + operating overhead.**

**Cost per accepted record = total workflow cost ÷ accepted records.**

Keep the categories separate even if some are initially unknown. An unknown cost should be shown as an assumption to investigate rather than quietly set to zero.

The acceptance rule also needs a clear definition. A searchable document, a complete invoice and an audited financial record can have very different quality requirements. The same parser can therefore have different cost per accepted record in different applications.

## Worked example: 10,000 documents a month

Consider a hypothetical monthly workload of 10,000 documents. Suppose its modeled processing cost is \$300, retries cost \$20, review costs \$900 and operating overhead allocated to the workflow is \$180. Total cost is \$1,400.

If 9,500 documents meet the acceptance rule, cost per accepted record is approximately \$0.147. These numbers are invented solely to demonstrate the calculation; they are not Datalab or LlamaIndex prices or measured review rates.

Now suppose a different configuration raises processing cost by \$100 but reduces review cost by \$250 while preserving the same accepted-record count. The second configuration would reduce total cost by \$150 despite a higher processing line item.

If the more expensive mode leaves review time unchanged, the extra processing spend needs another justification. Record correction time during the trial so the calculation can answer that question.

## Assumptions to put beside the estimate

| Assumption | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Pages per document | Page pricing does not directly equal document pricing |
| Operations performed | Parsing, extraction and other tasks can be distinct |
| Mode and optional features | Different configurations may have different charges |
| Retry policy | Failed or repeated work can change total usage |
| Review time and labor rate | Small correction burdens can dominate processing cost |
| Acceptance rule | A cheaper output may serve a less demanding task |
| Contract and retention settings | Published benchmark prices may use different terms |

Datalab’s OmniParseBench materials identify a data-retention discount in their historical pricing chart. A comparison using those chart prices should preserve that condition instead of presenting them as unconditional list prices. [OmniParseBench pricing notes](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench).

Apply the same discipline to LlamaIndex. Use the actual plan and configuration being evaluated, not a convenient price from a different tier.

## How should self-hosting be costed?

Self-hosted inference has a different cost structure from an API. It can include hardware or cloud compute, idle capacity, storage, deployment engineering, monitoring and upgrade work. License terms may also affect eligibility or commercial cost.

Include the actual work required to operate a public checkpoint. Estimate engineering time from the proposed deployment and the team’s existing infrastructure rather than assigning a generic staffing penalty.

Use measured utilization where possible. A GPU dedicated to a small intermittent workload has a different cost per page from the same GPU kept busy with a scheduled batch. Report the utilization assumption and explain how it was estimated.

For staffing, separate existing shared infrastructure from new work caused by the project. That keeps the analysis useful to a buyer who already operates models in production.

## Deciding which configuration is economical

Check whether the cheaper Datalab modes meet the acceptance rule for routine document groups. Reserve more expensive processing for the groups where it measurably reduces rejection or correction work.

For a LlamaIndex option, populate the worksheet with its own measured processing and correction costs. If both configurations meet the acceptance rule with the same review effort, a lower processing price represents a real saving.

Before approving the budget, recalculate it with twice the document length, review time or volume. The changes show which assumptions deserve closer measurement.

Put LlamaExtract Agentic in the cost-and-quality trial using the benchmarked pipeline as the starting point. Replace recorded benchmark costs with your actual quote, then add measured retries and review work. Choose on cost per accepted document and disclose unresolved outputs alongside the accepted ones.

title: "Marker 2 vs LiteParse and LlamaParse: Local Parsing or a Managed API?"
description: "Start with LiteParse when you want a local parsing path; evaluate LlamaParse when difficult tables, charts and layout justify a managed document-processing service."

---

# Marker 2 vs LiteParse and LlamaParse: Local Parsing or a Managed API?

Start with LiteParse when you want a local parsing path; evaluate LlamaParse when difficult tables, charts and layout justify a managed document-processing service. Marker 2 is the Datalab alternative to compare against those choices. The decision is how much document understanding and operating work your application needs, rather than which vendor offers more processing modes.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Product facts reflect research through October 28, 2026. No new performance benchmark is reported here.*

## Which LlamaIndex option should you choose?

| Need | LlamaIndex starting point | What to verify against Marker 2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local text and spatial parsing | LiteParse | Text order, coordinates, OCR setup and maintenance |
| Hard charts, tables and page layout | LlamaParse | The selected tier’s output on the difficult pages |
| Schema-guided fields and repeated records | LlamaParse Extract / LlamaExtract | Record accuracy, missing values and supporting evidence |

LiteParse is a local parsing tool; LlamaParse is a separate commercial processing service. That gives a team two LlamaIndex paths to evaluate without claiming they have identical capabilities. [LiteParse](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse), [LlamaParse documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/).

There is no matched Marker 2-versus-LiteParse result in this draft. LlamaParse’s ParseBench score should not be assigned to LiteParse or treated as a measured Marker 2 comparison.

## How does Marker 2 process a PDF?

Marker 2 combines embedded PDF text with layout analysis and selective use of a vision-language model. Its release describes different fast and balanced paths, plus an option that disables OCR. It uses Surya where the native-text path needs help rather than necessarily invoking full-page recognition for every document. [Marker 2 release](https://api.datalab.to/blog/marker-2), [Marker repository](https://github.com/datalab-to/marker).

A reliable text layer can save the work of visually transcribing every character. Check it before relying on it, though: selectable text can still come out incomplete or in the wrong order.

PDFs can contain broken character mappings, invisible duplicate text or scanned pages mixed with digital pages. A pipeline needs a way to recognize those conditions. The quality of that routing decision can matter as much as the quality of the OCR model used after escalation.

## Where LiteParse fits

LiteParse is a local parsing tool, with documented local OCR behavior and options for external OCR servers. It is a separate artifact from OCRia and the LlamaParse commercial service. Evaluating LiteParse does not evaluate all of LlamaIndex’s document-processing capabilities. [LiteParse repository](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse).

The same distinction applies to Marker and Datalab’s broader platform. A local converter, an OCR model and a managed service can share a vendor while solving different operational problems.

| Architecture | Attractive when | Main question to test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Native-text-first | Digital text is reliable | Is reading order and meaning preserved? |
| Selective OCR | Most pages are easy, some require repair | Does escalation catch the difficult cases? |
| Full-page visual processing | Layout and visual evidence dominate | Is the extra processing justified by better usable output? |
| Managed pipeline | The team prefers a service contract | Does the end-to-end result meet quality and operating requirements? |

These categories overlap. A managed product may combine several approaches, while a local tool may support optional components. Describe the tested configuration rather than assigning a permanent architectural label to an entire company.

## Routing a mixed collection of manuals

Consider a hypothetical repository of 1,000 technical manuals. Most pages contain selectable text, but some appendices are scans and a few equations are images. Running every page through the most expensive path may be unnecessary. Running no OCR may omit important material.

A selective workflow could extract native text, inspect the result, and route suspect pages or regions for additional processing. It should preserve a record of that decision so an engineer can understand why a page took longer or produced a different representation.

Test the routing policy against labeled cases. Include pages that look clean but have faulty text extraction. Include pages with very little text that are legitimately sparse, so the system does not escalate every cover page or photograph.

## What should a fair Marker-versus-LiteParse test measure?

Begin with the same source files and the same output requirements. If an application only needs searchable text, it should not silently grade a tool on chart interpretation. If it needs table structure, plain text completeness alone is insufficient.

Measure at least four outcomes:

1. **Content preservation:** important text, numbers and symbols survive.
2. **Structural usefulness:** reading order and table relationships support the application.
3. **Operating behavior:** latency, memory use, failures and required dependencies are recorded.
4. **Escalation cost:** difficult pages receive additional work without excessive false alarms.

Record hardware and OCR settings. A CPU-only configuration and a GPU-backed configuration answer different deployment questions. Their results can both be useful, but should not be presented as if the software alone caused every difference.

Keep failed and partially processed documents in the report. Excluding them can make a cheap pipeline appear more effective than it is for a real ingestion job.

## When the extra visual processing earns its cost

Take documents where the cheaper path struggles and inspect what the full-page VLM recovers. The additional processing is worth paying for when the recovered information changes whether you can use the document.

For example, better visual handling may matter if a scientific application needs an equation associated with its surrounding explanation. It may matter less for a document inventory that only needs title, author and a searchable text preview.

Divide the additional cost by the number of extra documents that become usable. Include any change in human correction time. Maintaining several processing routes also takes engineering work, which can outweigh savings on model calls in a small deployment.

## Choosing how much infrastructure to own

For mostly digital documents, begin with LiteParse as the LlamaIndex local option and compare the selected Marker configuration on the same output contract. Route the difficult subset into a separate LlamaParse trial when local parsing loses required structure. This is an architecture recommendation; no matched local-tool accuracy or speed winner is claimed.

Operating either local tool leaves the team responsible for installation, monitoring and failures. Compare that work with the service contract offered by LlamaParse or Datalab before deciding to own the stack.

Start with LiteParse for a local parsing trial and add LlamaParse when difficult pages need a richer processing path. Compare Marker 2 against the specific path you would deploy. Retain clean digital PDFs, scans and mixed-content files in separate groups so that a local-tool decision does not hide the hard-document failures.

# Best document parsers for RAG in 2026

*Disclosure: LlamaIndex makes LlamaParse and LiteParse and built ParseBench. This comparison uses published parsing results and linked project documentation. Parsing scores measure document conversion, not retrieval or answer accuracy.*

**What is the best PDF parser for RAG?** Our overall recommendation is LlamaParse, based on its parsing quality, source structure and choice of deployment options. Agentic Plus leads this ParseBench comparison at 86.69 overall; Agentic scores 82.83 at a recorded \$12.50 per 1,000 pages. LlamaParse works with your chosen retriever, model and framework, and also supports document processing beyond RAG, including extraction for insurance and financial workflows.

- **Most accurate managed parser:** LlamaParse Agentic Plus, 86.69 overall and 92.19 on charts
- **Best value for mixed PDFs:** LlamaParse Agentic, 82.83 at \$12.50 per 1,000 pages
- **Free and local:** LiteParse, PyMuPDF4LLM or Docling
- **Scanned PDFs:** LlamaParse Agentic
- **Coding agents and lightweight first passes:** LiteParse
- **Must run in your own cloud:** LlamaParse BYOC or Reducto Full VPC

## Why prioritize LlamaParse in a RAG ingestion trial?

The pinned ParseBench results support a clear parsing-quality case. LlamaParse Agentic scores 82.83 overall, versus 73.50 for Extend 2.0 and 70.87 for Reducto Agentic. Agentic Plus adds a chart result of 92.19, versus 76.02 and 72.37 for those same competitor rows. For a corpus whose answers depend on chart values and table context, those are concrete reasons to start the ingestion trial with LlamaParse. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv).

Then hold chunking, embeddings and retrieval settings constant and measure the questions your users actually ask. A parsing advantage is evidence for selecting an ingestion candidate; it is not a measured RAG answer-accuracy uplift.

The table uses the [ParseBench leaderboard](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv) at commit 0ccc167 (November 2, 2026). Overall, tables and charts are scores on a 0–100 scale. API costs reflect the **benchmark configuration**, converted to dollars per 1,000 pages, rather than a vendor's cheapest advertised tier. Local processing costs depend on hardware and throughput.

## What do these results measure?

ParseBench evaluates roughly 2,000 human-verified enterprise pages across tables, charts, content faithfulness, semantic formatting and visual grounding. Overall is the mean of those five dimensions, not the share of RAG questions answered correctly. The [repository](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench) provides evaluation code, pipeline definitions and links to published outputs. These results help shortlist parsers by the document content they preserve.

## What makes a parser good for RAG?

Look for five things in its output:

- **Reading order:** paragraphs stay together across columns instead of becoming interleaved sentences.
- **Table structure:** headers, values and merged cells retain their relationships.
- **Usable figure content:** charts contribute searchable labels, descriptions or values to a text-based index.
- **Headings:** sections remain identifiable so chunking can preserve their context.
- **Source locations:** page numbers and bounding boxes let users inspect the evidence behind an answer.

A financial table needs its year headers attached to each value. Retrieving the numbers alone can still support the wrong answer.

## Which managed parsers should you evaluate?

### LlamaParse

[LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse) converts documents into structured content through a standalone API that works with any LLM or framework. Agentic is a practical starting tier for mixed PDFs, scoring 82.83 overall at \$12.50 per 1,000 benchmark pages. Agentic Plus improves tables and charts; Cost Effective reduces the page price. You still choose how to chunk and retrieve the output. For example, a LangChain pipeline can parse with LlamaParse, split by Markdown headings and index the chunks in its existing vector store.

### Reducto

[Reducto](https://docs.reducto.ai/) combines parsing with configurable chunking and deployment options. Its Agentic row scores 70.87 overall and 72.37 on charts, making it worth evaluating when figures must become retrievable content. The benchmark cost is \$47.60 per 1,000 pages for that configuration. Compare the exact parsing mode and returned chunks rather than applying a cheaper product's list price to this score. Its [deployment documentation](https://docs.reducto.ai/onprem/enterprise_deployment_options) distinguishes hybrid from Full VPC deployments. See [LlamaParse vs Reducto](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-reducto).

### Extend

[Extend](https://docs.extend.ai/) includes parsing within a broader document workflow platform. The Extend 2.0 configuration scores 73.50 overall and 76.02 on charts, at a benchmark cost of \$25 per 1,000 pages. It belongs on a shortlist when parsing feeds document review or extraction workflows as well as retrieval. These results apply to the Extend 2.0 configuration. For deployment-sensitive work, its BYOC and hybrid options have different inference boundaries. See [LlamaParse vs Extend](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-extend-ai).

### Mistral OCR

[Mistral OCR](https://docs.mistral.ai/capabilities/document_ai/basic_ocr) is an OCR-first API for turning documents into text and structured output. The OCR 4 row scores 58.38 overall at \$4 per 1,000 pages, with 74.03 on tables and 1.86 on charts. That makes its low price more relevant to text-heavy documents than to recovering chart values. The leaderboard has a separate Annotation configuration; do not combine that configuration's scores with the standard OCR row's cost.

## Which local parsers are worth trying?

### Docling

[Docling](https://github.com/docling-project/docling) is an open-source document conversion toolkit. Its document representation preserves structure and provenance, and its [hierarchical and hybrid chunkers](https://docling-project.github.io/docling/concepts/chunking/) help turn that structure into retrieval units. The code is MIT licensed; check model licenses separately. No comparable ParseBench score is available for its default setup, so test it on your own documents. See [LlamaParse vs Docling](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-docling).

### PyMuPDF4LLM

[PyMuPDF4LLM](https://github.com/pymupdf/pymupdf4llm) is a practical baseline for born-digital PDFs. It scores 50.47 overall and 56.93 on tables, but only 1.63 on charts. Use it when extracting embedded text is the main job, then inspect reading order and headers on harder pages. Its packaging has moved into `pymupdf`; consult the current installation instructions. Check the AGPL or commercial license before incorporating it into a product.

### Marker, including Datalab's model options

[Marker](https://github.com/datalab-to/marker) produces Markdown, JSON, HTML and chunks from a local model pipeline. It is worth evaluating for scans and structured documents when you can operate the inference stack. Datalab also develops Chandra-ocr-2, a separate model with a 70.59 overall and 89.20 table score; those results do not describe Marker. Marker code is Apache 2.0; its model weights have separate commercial conditions. Treat the local software and Datalab's managed service as different configurations.

### MinerU

[MinerU](https://github.com/opendatalab/MinerU) offers model-based conversion for documents with substantial layout and OCR requirements. Its verified MinerU2.5-Pro configuration scores 69.27 overall and 59.12 on charts. That is evidence for the named model configuration, not every release or CPU backend. Budget for model inference and benchmark throughput on your hardware. The repository license adds commercial thresholds and online-service attribution requirements to Apache 2.0 terms.

### Unstructured OSS

[Unstructured's open-source library](https://github.com/Unstructured-IO/unstructured) partitions files into elements and supports chunking, including grouping by title. It fits pipelines that need a common ingestion interface for several file types. PDF strategy matters: fast text extraction and higher-resolution layout processing are different paths. No ParseBench score is listed for the OSS library here. Its hosted platform has different processing capabilities, so do not use hosted benchmark claims to describe the local package. See [LlamaParse vs Unstructured](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-unstructured).

### LiteParse

[LiteParse](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse) is LlamaIndex's Apache 2.0 local parser, with a Rust core, a CLI and bindings for several runtimes. It provides Markdown and spatial output without a cloud API or LLM call. Its submitted no-OCR score is 36.90 overall. Use it for a lightweight first pass on simpler documents, or to identify pages that need heavier processing. Its complexity check can support routing, but it does not prove that a page was parsed correctly.

## What about Azure, Google and AWS?

### Azure Document Intelligence

[Azure Layout](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/ai-services/document-intelligence/) scores 56.76 overall and 85.97 on tables. Its 1.27 chart score is a limitation for text-based RAG that needs chart data. It is worth considering when Azure integration or supported container deployment is a key requirement. Confirm the model version available in your chosen deployment. See [LlamaParse vs Azure Document Intelligence](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-azure-document-intelligence).

### Google Document AI

[Google Document AI](https://cloud.google.com/document-ai) integrates with Google Cloud document workflows. The leaderboard row is Google's Layout Parser, run April 8, 2026, and scores 48.66 overall and 54.95 on tables. Processor version, region and output structure matter when selecting a deployment. See [LlamaParse vs Document AI](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-document-ai).

### Amazon Textract

[Textract](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/textract/) scores 84.46 on tables but 4.47 on charts, with 48.31 overall. It is useful to evaluate for AWS workflows centered on OCR, forms and tables. PrivateLink provides private access to the hosted service; it does not install Textract in your account. Add your own transformation and chunking for retrieval. See [LlamaParse vs Amazon Textract](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-amazon-textract).

## Which parser should you choose for your documents?

| Your corpus or constraint | Start with | What to validate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overall RAG document ingestion | LlamaParse | Content, tables, charts and source references |
| Scans and mixed layouts | LlamaParse Agentic | OCR and structure on the representative corpus |

| Lower processing budget | Compare LlamaParse Cost Effective and Agentic | Quality floor and cost per usable document |
| LangChain, a custom retriever or another framework | LlamaParse standalone API | Output and source references into the existing pipeline |

These recommendations keep LlamaParse as the overall production starting point and separate mandatory constraints from quality rankings. ParseBench measures parsing, not retrieval performance or a scan-only test; validate end-to-end answers with the rest of the RAG pipeline held constant.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is Docling good enough for RAG?

Evaluate Docling when local open-source execution is a requirement. For the overall production choice, start with LlamaParse’s published parsing evidence and compare the actual output on scans, spanning table headers, charts and multi-column pages. Local execution alone does not establish equivalent ingestion quality.

### Do I need OCR for RAG?

You need OCR when useful text exists only as pixels. Mixed PDFs may need OCR for some pages even if other pages have an embedded text layer.

### Should tables be Markdown, HTML or JSON?

Markdown works for simple rectangular tables. HTML can preserve row and column spans; structured JSON is useful when you need cell relationships and coordinates. Preserve those relationships when chunking.

### Can I send PDFs straight to GPT or Gemini?

Yes, especially for a small number of direct questions. Compare parsing quality and operational effort before building a reusable ingestion pipeline; see [Related article](/agents/llamaparse-vs-gpt-claude-and-gemini-for-pdf-parsing-2026).

### Is LlamaParse only for LlamaIndex users?

No. Its API output can feed LangChain, a custom retriever or another framework. You can keep your existing embedding model, vector database and answering model.

### How should I test a parser on my own documents?

Create questions whose answers depend on prose, tables, scans and figures. Change only the parser, keeping the rest of the RAG pipeline fixed, and measure retrieval of supporting evidence, answer correctness, citation quality, cost and latency.

[Try LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/pricing) with 10,000 free credits per month, or start locally with [LiteParse](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse).

# Reducto Chart Extraction vs LlamaParse: Numeric Accuracy and Source Context

LlamaParse Agentic Plus scores higher than the tested Reducto Agentic configuration on ParseBench charts. That is the relevant product comparison for buyers who need numerical chart answers. Keep Reducto r-1’s native figure descriptions separate from optional advanced chart extraction, and do not use an OCRia research result as a substitute for a configured LlamaParse API result.

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 93.27 | 92.19 | 75.43 |
| Reducto (Agentic) | 70.87 | 80.20 | 72.37 | 68.71 |
| Reducto (r-1) | 61.49 | 85.00 | 2.74 | 57.31 |

Agentic Plus scores 92.19 on charts versus 72.37 for the tested Reducto Agentic configuration. The much lower native r-1 chart result reflects that evaluated configuration; it does not prove a result for r-1 plus optional advanced chart extraction. A dedicated trial should name that option explicitly.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## Native descriptions and advanced numerical extraction

Reducto describes native r-1 figure output as a short description, while advanced chart extraction uses additional processing for numerical data. Its chart documentation covers geometry, OCR and legend mapping with a VLM fallback. It supports several chart types and identifies dense scatterplots as only partially supported. Reducto should therefore not be characterized as lacking numerical chart extraction. [Reducto chart extraction](https://docs.reducto.ai/configs/parse/chart-extraction)

LlamaIndex's OCRia-1 technical report evaluates chart understanding as part of document parsing research. That report is useful context for choosing tests, but it does not establish a direct Reducto product comparison. A model result and a configured API workflow are different evaluation objects. [OCRia-1 technical report](https://www.llamaindex.ai/ocria/ocria-1-technical-report.pdf)

Start by naming the expected output. Otherwise an inexpensive descriptive result can be unfairly compared with a more involved data-reconstruction workflow.

## Score labels and units alongside values

Separate the chart's components before scoring the final answer. The correct number attached to the wrong series is still wrong. A correctly reconstructed trend with the wrong units can mislead a business decision.

| Component | Example check |
| --- | --- |
| Series identity | Revenue and operating income remain distinct |
| Axis meaning | Percentages are not treated as currency |
| Time alignment | Each value belongs to the correct quarter |
| Numeric fidelity | Reconstructed values meet an agreed tolerance |
| Missing-data handling | Gaps are not silently interpolated as facts |
| Answer support | A downstream claim follows from recovered data |

Define tolerances before seeing vendor results. A chart with printed data labels may justify exact-value scoring. A rasterized curve without labels may require an error tolerance tied to source resolution and the intended use.

## Revenue rises while margin falls

Imagine a chart with revenue shown as bars on a left-hand dollar axis and margin shown as a line on a right-hand percentage axis. In this hypothetical example, revenue rises from \$100 million to \$120 million, while margin declines from 20% to 18%.

A general description might correctly say that revenue increased while margin fell. A numeric extraction must also preserve which values use dollars and which use percentages. If an application asks for operating profit, it needs to calculate \$20 million and \$21.6 million from the correctly paired inputs.

The apparent decline in margin does not mean operating profit declined. A useful evaluation checks the complete reasoning chain: extracted series, units, multiplication and final comparison. This scenario is not evidence of an error by Reducto or OCRia-1; it is a fixture that exposes what the task requires.

A test set should also include ordinary single-axis charts. Evaluating only unusually difficult figures can distort expectations for a workload dominated by straightforward visualizations.

## Use charts with known source data

Prefer charts with accessible source data so numeric truth does not depend entirely on a human reading pixels. Preserve the original data and the rendered chart separately. Include variation in labels, legends, scales, colors, resolution and surrounding page context.

Keep a development set for configuring each workflow. Freeze a held-out set before running the comparison. If one workflow needs an advanced option to meet the task, enable it and disclose the choice rather than excluding a legitimate capability.

Score both extraction and application answers. This helps distinguish a parsing error from a downstream arithmetic or retrieval error. Save intermediate results so a reviewer can trace an incorrect answer to its source.

## Price the configuration needed for the answer

Measure time to an accepted answer, including any required advanced processing. A base figure description and a reconstructed data table do not represent equivalent work. Report both configurations if both are relevant to buyers.

Pricing needs particular care. The reviewed Reducto rate card lists optional chart-related charges, while the chart documentation contains language suggesting advanced steps add latency without extra cost. Confirm the applicable account pricing before publishing a numerical workflow comparison. A documentation discrepancy is a reason to verify the quote, not evidence of hidden billing. [Reducto usage and pricing](https://docs.reducto.ai/reference/credit-usage)

For both vendors, separate API charges from review costs. A cheap result requiring manual reconstruction may be expensive for the workflow; an advanced result may be unnecessary if the application only needs a caption.

## Match the output to the question

For discovery and broad summaries, descriptive output may be sufficient. Calculations and period comparisons need numerical evidence with the correct units and series labels. More processing is worthwhile when it supplies information the application actually uses.

Include Reducto’s advanced chart option in a numerical evaluation rather than comparing only its base description. Likewise, record the selected LlamaParse configuration and any downstream calculation steps. LlamaIndex publishes this guide; the OCRia-1 paper does not establish a Reducto head-to-head result, and no new comparative measurements are presented here.

## What if the source chart only permits an estimate?

Define an acceptable tolerance before running the test. A value read from an unlabeled raster curve should not be treated like a printed data label. State when the result is an estimate and check whether that precision is adequate for the question.

Prioritize LlamaParse Agentic Plus for numerical chart parsing based on the published chart-score advantage. Include the exact Reducto chart-enabled configuration you would deploy, and test known values, series, units and estimation tolerances. A product-level parsing result is stronger evidence than transferring a model-only score.

title: "Extend Classify vs LlamaParse Classify: Routing Mixed Document Packets"
description: "Compare LlamaParse Classify with Extend’s current classification options, routing rules, confidence and review handling for mixed document packets."
published: "2026-10-10"
updated: "2026-11-16"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/classify/"

# Extend Classify vs LlamaParse Classify: Routing Mixed Document Packets

LlamaParse Classify provides a documented classification API that uses natural-language rules and returns a type, confidence and reasoning. Compare that product directly with Extend Classify, then use Split when a single packet contains several documents. The buying question is which configured intake path routes the right pages into schema-specific extraction.

*Published by LlamaIndex. The packet example is hypothetical, and this article does not report comparative classification accuracy.*

## Compare the documented LlamaParse Classify API

LlamaParse Classify accepts rules describing the document types to identify and returns a predicted type, confidence and reasoning for each file. This gives buyers a specific LlamaIndex product to evaluate before extraction, rather than an unspecified custom classifier. [Classify documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/classify/).

For mixed packets, evaluate the separate Split API to create logical document segments before routing them into extraction. Split is documented as beta and subject to breaking changes. [Split documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/split/).

Neither ParseBench nor ExtractBench measures routing accuracy. Compare rule definitions, page coverage, unknown handling and downstream accepted records on the same labeled packets.

## What changed in Extend Classify?

Extend’s November 13, 2026 release introduced Classification Instant at 0.1 credits per page and made Classification Standard 1.2.0 the default. Both return numerical confidence. These are current product options to include in a trial; they do not establish comparative routing accuracy. Confirm the selected configuration and price in the account being evaluated. [Extend’s changelog](https://docs.extend.ai/2026-02-09/changelog/2026/11/13).

## What does Extend Classify return?

The Classify contract returns one matched category with confidence and reasoning. Extend recommends routing on a stable category ID rather than the editable type name. It also describes Split as the capability for separating bundled documents. [Classification overview](https://docs.extend.ai/classification/overview), [splitting overview](https://docs.extend.ai/splitting/overview).

Single-label classification is a useful design when one input represents one document. It becomes a source of confusion when a file is treated as a document even though the upload contains several independent records.

Represent the upload and its constituent documents separately in the application model. That preserves the packet relationship without forcing every page to share one type.

## What can go wrong with a mixed packet?

Consider a hypothetical five-page upload:

| Pages | Contents | Intended action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1–2 | Supplier invoice | Extract payable amount and line items |
| 3 | Purchase order | Match order identifiers and authorized items |
| 4 | Delivery receipt | Check delivered quantities |
| 5 | Cover letter | Retain as context or send to a separate route |

Calling the whole file an invoice does not describe every item inside it. Sending all five pages to an invoice extractor may also create ambiguity when the purchase order repeats quantities and prices that differ from the final invoice.

The packet is hypothetical; no Extend routing failure is being reported. It illustrates two possible designs: split the documents to create distinct records, or preserve their relationship for a joint matching decision. Either way, make each document's role explicit.

## How should the intake decision be organized?

A useful intake policy asks three questions in order:

1. Is the input expected to contain one business document or a packet?
2. Are document boundaries known, inferred or still uncertain?
3. Which next action is appropriate for each resulting unit?

The answers should produce an explicit route. A known single invoice can go directly to classification or a configured extractor. A mixed packet may need splitting followed by per-document classification. An uncertain upload can enter a review route before expensive downstream work starts.

Do not rely on a filename as the only source of truth. A file called “invoice.pdf” can contain attachments or an incorrectly assembled scan. Filename hints may help, but the application's acceptance contract should state whether they are trusted.

## How should unknown categories be handled?

Define an unknown or “other” route deliberately. It should lead to a meaningful action, such as review, retention without extraction or a generic fallback whose output is not automatically trusted.

A catch-all category is most useful when its downstream behavior is explicit. If every unknown input silently enters the invoice extractor, the category may exist in the configuration without providing operational protection.

Treat ambiguous cases separately from genuinely new types. A blurred invoice might belong to a known category but lack enough readable evidence. A new customs form may be clear yet absent from the taxonomy. Both can need review, but they imply different improvements to the pipeline.

Track those reasons. Otherwise, a team may keep expanding category descriptions when the real problem is scan quality, or improve image processing when the missing piece is a new document class.

## What should routing quality measure?

A confusion matrix is a useful starting point, but the consequences of its cells differ. Confusing an invoice with a credit note may have a larger operational effect than confusing two informational attachments.

Assign consequences to wrong routes before inspecting vendor results. Measure whether the mistake produces an obvious rejection, an unnecessary review or an apparently valid but wrong downstream record. The last outcome deserves particular attention because it can evade monitoring based only on failed jobs.

Also measure recovery. Can the workflow identify that the selected extractor's output violates basic expectations? Can it redirect the document without creating a duplicate downstream record? A resilient intake design combines classification with checks on the result it enables.

## How do stable IDs improve operational safety?

Treat category IDs as interface contracts and category descriptions as configuration. A human-friendly name can change during tuning without requiring every downstream branch to be renamed. Extend explicitly distinguishes stable IDs from prompt-facing category text. [Classification routing guidance](https://docs.extend.ai/classification/overview).

Before deploying a taxonomy change, inspect branch coverage. Every category that can be returned should have an intended destination. A test suite should include renamed categories, new categories and unknown inputs, not only common happy-path documents.

## Where do Extend and LlamaIndex fit?

Extend's combination of classification, splitting and workflows is a meaningful strength for teams that want those decisions within one platform. A comparison should acknowledge that breadth rather than portraying a single-label endpoint as a packet-processing deficiency.

Use the same packet in a LlamaIndex comparison and inspect the records that reach the downstream system. Count wrong destinations and duplicate records as well as classification errors. If the source already guarantees a single known document type, also test whether classification adds enough value to justify the extra step.

## Sketch one packet's route before tuning the classifier

Start the intake trial with the documented LlamaParse Classify and Split APIs, then connect the selected source pages to schema-specific extraction. Measure wrong destinations, missed documents and accepted records against the corresponding vendor configuration. Keep Split’s beta status visible; no routing-accuracy superiority is established by the extraction benchmarks.

title: "How to convert PDFs to Markdown locally with LiteParse (2026)"
description: "Convert PDFs to Markdown on your own machine with LiteParse: one command, built-in OCR, Office files, Python, Node and browser support, and a coding-agent skill. Free and open source."
published: "2026-09-04"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/liteparse/"

# How to convert PDFs to Markdown locally with LiteParse (2026)

*Disclosure: LiteParse is an open-source project from LlamaIndex, which also makes LlamaParse.*

**How do you convert a PDF to Markdown locally?** Install LiteParse and run one command. It runs on your machine with no LLM, no API key and no cloud service, and it is free under the Apache 2.0 license.

```bash
npm i -g @llamaindex/liteparse
lit parse document.pdf --format markdown -o document.md
```

- **Install:** npm, pip or cargo, with the same `lit` command in each
- **Output:** Markdown with headings, tables, lists, images and links, or plain text, or JSON with bounding boxes
- **Scanned pages:** built-in Tesseract OCR, used only on embedded images and pages with no text layer
- **Other formats:** Word, PowerPoint and Excel through LibreOffice; PNG, JPG and other images natively
- **Where it runs:** the command line, Node.js/TypeScript, Python, Rust and the browser (WASM)
- **Coding agents:** a skill for Claude Code, Cursor and Codex
- **Hard documents:** dense tables, charts and difficult scans go to LlamaParse

## How do I install LiteParse?

Pick the package for your stack. Every package except the browser build includes the `lit` command-line tool.

```bash
# Node.js / TypeScript
npm i -g @llamaindex/liteparse

# Python
pip install liteparse

# Rust
cargo install liteparse

# Browser (WASM), no CLI
npm i @llamaindex/liteparse-wasm
```

Office files also need LibreOffice. PDFs and images need nothing else.

## How do I convert a PDF to Markdown?

```bash
lit parse document.pdf --format markdown -o document.md
```

LiteParse rebuilds headings, tables, lists, images and links from the page layout. It strips running headers and footers by default, because page numbers and repeated titles break up the text when you chunk it for retrieval.

| Task | Command |
| --- | --- |
| Print Markdown to the terminal | `lit parse document.pdf --format markdown` |
| Convert only some pages | `lit parse document.pdf --format markdown --target-pages "1-5,10"` |
| Save embedded images next to the Markdown | `lit parse document.pdf --format markdown --extract-images --image-output-dir ./images` |
| Leave images out | `lit parse document.pdf --format markdown --image-mode off` |
| Keep headers and footers | `lit parse document.pdf --format markdown --keep-headers-footers` |
| Convert a whole folder | `lit batch-parse ./pdfs ./markdown --format markdown` |

## How do I convert scanned PDFs?

Use the same command. LiteParse bundles Tesseract and runs OCR only on embedded images and pages with no text layer, so text-based pages stay fast.

```bash
lit parse scan.pdf --format markdown -o scan.md

# Scans in another language
lit parse scan.pdf --format markdown --ocr-language fra
```

On offline or air-gapped machines, download the Tesseract language files ahead of time and point LiteParse at them with `TESSDATA_PREFIX` or `--tessdata-path`. For higher OCR accuracy, run an OCR server such as EasyOCR or PaddleOCR (the repository includes ready-made servers) and pass `--ocr-server-url`.

## How do I use it from Python or TypeScript?

```py
from liteparse import LiteParse

parser = LiteParse(output_format="markdown")
result = parser.parse("document.pdf")
print(result.text)
```

```ts
import { LiteParse } from "@llamaindex/liteparse";

const parser = new LiteParse({ outputFormat: "markdown" });
const result = await parser.parse("document.pdf");
console.log(result.text);
```

Both libraries accept raw bytes as well as file paths, so you can parse uploads without writing them to disk. In the browser, the WASM package parses a `Uint8Array`. It has no built-in Tesseract, so OCR in the browser needs your own engine.

## Can it convert Word, PowerPoint and Excel files?

Yes. LiteParse converts Office files to PDF with LibreOffice, then parses them the same way. That covers .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, .odt, .csv and other formats. Images such as PNG, JPG and TIFF are converted natively and read with OCR.

```bash
lit parse report.docx --format markdown -o report.md
```

## How do I let a coding agent read PDFs?

Add the LiteParse skill to Claude Code, Cursor, Codex or another compatible agent:

```bash
npx skills add run-llama/llamaparse-agent-skills --skill liteparse
```

The skill needs Node 18 or later and the `lit` command. It teaches the agent to parse a document once to a file and search that file, instead of re-parsing it and pasting whole pages into its context.

## Can I get bounding boxes?

Yes. JSON output returns every text line with its position on the page, which you can use to highlight sources or build citations.

```bash
lit parse document.pdf --format json -o document.json
```

## When should I use LlamaParse instead?

LiteParse uses rules, not models. It handles prose, headings, lists and simple to moderate tables well. For dense or multi-level tables, complex multi-column layouts, charts and difficult scans, [LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse) gives more accurate results. For example, it returns chart values as tables.

You don't have to guess which documents need it. `lit is-complex` checks each page before parsing and flags scanned pages, garbled text, multi-column layouts, likely tables and dense figures. It exits with an error code when any page needs OCR, so you can use it in a script:

```bash
# Parse locally only when no page needs OCR
lit is-complex document.pdf --quiet && lit parse document.pdf --no-ocr --format markdown -o document.md
```

Send the documents it flags to LlamaParse. The free plan includes 10,000 credits per month.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is LiteParse free?

Yes. It is open source under the Apache 2.0 license and runs on your own machine, with no API key or usage fees.

### Does LiteParse use an LLM?

No. It reconstructs Markdown with rules, using PDFium to read text and Tesseract for OCR. Nothing is sent to a model or a cloud service.

### Does it work offline?

Yes. Tesseract downloads its language data on first use. On air-gapped machines, provide the language files yourself with `TESSDATA_PREFIX`.

### How fast is it?

Native text parsing takes about 2 to 5 ms per page, according to the project README. Pages that need OCR take longer. LiteParse OCRs pages in parallel, using one fewer worker than your CPU core count by default.

### Is LiteParse an open-source version of LlamaParse?

LiteParse is the team’s open-source local parsing tool. LlamaParse is the production document-processing platform for parsing and schema-guided extraction across routine and difficult documents. Choose it for its output quality and operating fit, independently of whether the application uses the LlamaIndex framework.

Get [LiteParse on GitHub](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse) or read the [LiteParse docs](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/liteparse/). For harder documents, [try LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/pricing) with 10,000 free credits per month.

title: "Can LlamaParse run on-premises?"
