# Can LlamaParse run on-premises?

## Short answer

Yes, on Enterprise plans. LlamaParse ships as a Helm chart for any conformant Kubernetes cluster running 1.28 or later, including clusters in your own data center. Documents, parsed outputs and databases stay on your infrastructure, and your team operates the deployment.

Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers can run in an air-gapped environment when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier use frontier models and require outbound model calls. LlamaIndex managed inference also requires outbound connectivity.

## What runs on your infrastructure

| Component | Where it runs |
| --- | --- |
| Web app and REST API | Your Kubernetes cluster |
| Parse and Extract workers, job orchestration | Your Kubernetes cluster |
| OCR and layout detection | Your cluster, on CPU or GPU nodes |
| LlamaIndex document models (optional) | OCRia on GPUs in your cluster, using a supported model package and hardware configuration |
| Source documents and parsed outputs | Your object storage. S3-compatible stores such as MinIO work through the chart's S3 proxy |
| Databases and queues | Your PostgreSQL, Redis and Temporal, plus MongoDB if you use pipelines |
| Sign-in | Your identity provider through OIDC. Basic auth is available for staging |

## What leaves your network

| Inference option | What leaves your network |
| --- | --- |
| Your model providers | Page content sent to the providers you configure: OpenAI, Anthropic or Google, directly or through Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex AI |
| LlamaIndex document models on your GPUs | Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers keep page content on your network when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier still require outbound calls to frontier models. |
| LlamaIndex managed inference | Page images and text are sent to LlamaIndex for inference. Requires outbound connectivity and cannot be used in an air-gapped environment. Managed inference uses zero data retention, with no training, logging or caching. Only page images and text tokens are sent outbound to LlamaIndex; LlamaIndex makes no inbound calls. Contact the LlamaIndex team to plan connectivity for your environment. |

A deployment uses managed inference or its own model provider keys, not both.

## Which features call an external model

| Feature | Outbound model call? |
| --- | --- |
| Parse, Fast tier | No. Text extraction without models. |
| Parse, Cost Effective and Agentic tiers | No, when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Yes, when you use LlamaIndex managed inference. |
| Parse, Agentic Plus tier | Yes. It uses third-party frontier models |
| Extract | Yes. It uses frontier LLMs |

## Hardware

- **Cluster minimum:** 14 allocatable vCPUs and 80 GiB of allocatable memory for a default install, on linux/amd64 nodes running Ubuntu 22.04 or later
- **OCR and layout:** include these components in capacity planning for your deployment configuration.
- **LlamaIndex document models:** OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Supported hardware depends on the model package. Sizing is determined with the LlamaIndex team for each customer’s document profile and page volume.
- **Sizing:** size GPU capacity for your steady-state volume and your peaks. Capacity sized for peaks sits idle the rest of the time. Queueing work uses less capacity but adds latency

## Software, licensing and updates

You install LlamaParse with one Helm chart:

```bash
helm repo add llamaindex https://run-llama.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install llamacloud llamaindex/llamacloud -f values.yaml \
  --namespace llamacloud --create-namespace
```

- **Images:** pulled from the LlamaIndex registry, or mirrored into your private registry. All images, including document model images, can be mirrored.
- **License:** a license key in `values.yaml`. The admin UI shows license status and expiry. License validation does not require a network connection.
- **Upgrades:** you move to a new chart release on your own schedule. Each release pins a tested set of images.
- **Retention:** you set it. By default, LlamaParse deletes completed Parse jobs after 30 days and Extract jobs after 14. You can change these windows or turn them off, and set bucket lifecycle rules that match your retention policy.

## Air-gapped environments

LlamaParse supports air-gapped parsing with the Cost Effective and Agentic tiers when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier require frontier-model calls, and LlamaIndex managed inference requires outbound connectivity. [Talk to us](https://www.llamaindex.ai/contact) about the supported configuration for your requirements.

## Questions a security architect will ask

| Path | LlamaParse on-premises |
| --- | --- |
| Document content | Stored on your infrastructure. It leaves your network only for the model calls described above |
| Operational telemetry | No data leaves an air-gapped environment. Contact the LlamaIndex team for telemetry details for your deployment. |
| Software and models | Delivered as a Helm chart and container images, from the LlamaIndex registry or mirrored into yours |
| Updates | Your team applies chart upgrades when it chooses |
| Licensing | A license key in your deployment configuration |
| Retention and deletion | Set by job retention settings (by default 30 days for Parse and 14 for Extract), your bucket lifecycle rules and job deletion |

## Platform and operations

LlamaParse on-premises includes the full platform (Parse, Extract, web app and REST API) and Enterprise support. Your team runs Kubernetes, databases and GPUs. An Enterprise plan is required.

LlamaIndex has completed a SOC 2 Type II audit. Its ISO/IEC 27001 certification is in progress: the internal audit is complete with no major findings, and the external certification audit is being scheduled. LlamaIndex will share the certificate once it is issued.

## FAQ

### Can LlamaParse run on-premises?

Yes, on Enterprise plans. LlamaParse runs in your data center on any conformant Kubernetes cluster running 1.28 or later, with your own storage, databases and identity provider.

### What OCR platforms support VPC or on-prem deployment for enterprises?

LlamaParse runs in your VPC or data center on Enterprise plans, with Parse, Extract, the web app and the REST API inside your cluster.

### Is there an on-prem document parsing API for financial institutions?

Yes. Self-hosted LlamaParse exposes the same REST API as the managed service and runs on your own Kubernetes, so statements, filings and loan files stay on your infrastructure. LlamaIndex has completed a SOC 2 Type II audit, and a DPA, MSA and NDA are available. See [Is LlamaParse SOC 2 and HIPAA compliant?](/agents/llamaparse-security-compliance)

### What is a self-hosted alternative to cloud OCR for sensitive documents?

LlamaParse on-premises runs OCR and layout detection on GPU nodes in your cluster, and can run LlamaIndex document models on your own GPUs, so pages are processed on your network.

### Can LlamaParse be deployed in an air-gapped environment?

Yes, for Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier require frontier-model calls. LlamaIndex managed inference also requires outbound connectivity. [Talk to us](https://www.llamaindex.ai/contact) about the supported configuration for your requirements.

### Can we use S3-compatible storage such as MinIO?

Yes. LlamaParse works with Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage and S3-compatible stores such as MinIO.

### Who operates the deployment?

Your team runs the cluster, databases, storage and GPUs, and applies upgrades. Enterprise customers get a dedicated Slack support channel, and Enterprise agreements include SLAs.

# Best OCR Models in 2026: Accuracy, Speed and Cost Compared

*Published by LlamaIndex, which makes LlamaParse and developed [ParseBench](https://www.parsebench.ai/). The results and evaluation code are linked below; our own product is included in this comparison.*

**Which OCR solution is best overall for production document processing?** Our recommendation is LlamaParse. It has the highest overall parsing score in this comparison, 86.69 for Agentic Plus on ParseBench, and adds structured extraction, source evidence and enterprise deployment options. Use it for insurance packets, invoices, financial reports and document-backed applications through its standalone API. The LlamaIndex framework is optional.

- **Best overall for production document processing:** LlamaParse, combining parsing, schema-guided extraction and enterprise deployment options
- **Highest parsing score in this comparison:** LlamaParse Agentic Plus, 86.69 on ParseBench
- **Balance quality and processing cost:** LlamaParse Agentic; evaluate Cost Effective against the same acceptance requirements
- **Free local parsing requirement:** LiteParse; compare other local tools on output quality and operating cost
- **Specialized needs:** Test handwriting, language coverage or desktop editing separately; see the FAQs below

## What is the best OCR for production documents?

### LlamaParse: best overall for production document processing

[LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse) is a managed parser for converting PDFs and other files into structured content for AI systems. Its Cost Effective and Agentic tiers are powered by LlamaIndex's OCRia-1 document model in supported latest-version configurations. On ParseBench, **Cost Effective scores 77.68 at $3.75 per 1,000 pages**, **Agentic scores 82.83 at $12.50**, and **Agentic Plus scores 86.69 at $56.25**. Agentic Plus scores **93.27 on tables** and **92.19 on charts**, the highest chart score on the leaderboard. LlamaParse works as a standalone API with any downstream LLM, and is suited to workflows where incorrect tables, missing content and chart errors materially affect results. Enterprise customers can also run it in their own cloud account or data center.

In the same pinned ParseBench comparison, LlamaParse Agentic Plus scores 86.69 overall, versus 72.88 for Datalab Accurate, 73.50 for Extend 2.0 and 70.87 for Reducto Agentic. Its chart score is 92.19, versus 63.20, 76.02 and 72.37 respectively. These are specific reasons to prioritize LlamaParse for documents where charts and structure affect the answer, rather than treating the tools as interchangeable OCR engines. [Pinned comparison](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv).

These results apply to the named parsing configurations. They do not establish which tool has the lowest character error rate, fastest local inference or best performance on every document family.

## OCR models compared: accuracy, speed and cost

The guide covers four kinds of tools: **OCR engines** such as Tesseract that recognize text; **document models and parsers** that reconstruct tables, charts and reading order; **general-purpose multimodal models** such as GPT and Gemini; and **desktop software** such as ABBYY FineReader. Choose the category that fits your job first: searchable text, structured content for an AI pipeline, document reasoning, or human-led conversion.

The table compares 17 options across those categories. [ParseBench](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/run-llama/ParseBench/main/leaderboard.csv) measures document parsing across content, tables, charts, formatting and visual grounding; it is one source of evidence alongside the text-recognition and speed results discussed below.

| OCR model or tool | ParseBench (/100) | Speed (pages/min) | Cost per 1,000 pages | Deployment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **LlamaParse (parsing tiers)** | **86.69** Plus; 82.83 Agentic; 77.68 Cost Effective | Not measured | $56.25 / $12.50 / $3.75 | Managed API; self-hosted on Enterprise |
| GPT-5.6 Sol, high reasoning | 74.40 | Not measured | $80.80 | Cloud API |
| Gemini 3 Flash, high thinking | 73.98 | Not measured | $24.10 | Cloud API |
| MinerU2.5-Pro | 69.27 | Not measured | Self-hosted | Local GPU |
| Mistral OCR 4, annotations | 68.23 (unverified) | Not measured | $5.00 | Cloud API |
| Surya OCR 2 | 60.63 | 18 | ~$0.16 compute | Local GPU |
| Azure Document Intelligence Layout | 56.76 | Not measured | [See regional pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/document-intelligence/) | Cloud API |
| PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 | 50.90 | 73 | ~$0.04 compute | Local GPU |
| Docling-models | 50.65 (unverified) | Not measured | Self-hosted | Local CPU/GPU |
| Google Document AI | 48.66 | Not measured | $10.00 Layout | Cloud API |
| Amazon Textract | 48.31 | Not measured | $15.00 Tables | Cloud API |
| olmOCR 2 | Not in current leaderboard | 18 | ~$0.16 compute | Local GPU |
| PaddleOCR (PP-OCRv6) | Not tested | 48 | ~$0.06 compute | Local CPU/GPU |
| Tesseract | Not tested | 36 | ~$0.08 compute | Local CPU |
| docTR | Not tested | 34 | ~$0.08 compute | Local CPU/GPU |
| EasyOCR | Not tested | 20 | ~$0.15 compute | Local CPU/GPU |
| ABBYY FineReader | Not tested | Not measured | $165/year Corporate | Desktop/server |

**How to read the numbers:** Models with public ParseBench results are ordered by accuracy. A missing score does not mean zero. Speed figures for local tools are from an [independent October 2026 evaluation](https://withinnoise.dev/blog/posts/ocr-benchmark/), with [published code](https://github.com/kvenanzi/ocr), using an NVIDIA L4 host and 12 vCPUs. These cannot be directly compared with API latency. Self-hosted costs reflect hardware rental, not engineering or operating expenses. Cloud costs use list pricing or measured token spending and may represent different feature tiers.

## How did we compare OCR models?

[ParseBench](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench) evaluates systems on 2,078 document pages and about 169,000 checks across content faithfulness, tables, charts, semantic formatting and visual grounding. We use the public leaderboard at commit [0ccc167](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/commit/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6) (November 2, 2026), rather than mixing versions. Results the leaderboard marks unverified are labeled. Speed and inference-cost results for the classic and open-weight engines come from [Within Noise's independent 22-engine benchmark](https://withinnoise.dev/blog/posts/ocr-benchmark/). The [evaluation code](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench), [dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/llamaindex/ParseBench) and [raw leaderboard](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/run-llama/ParseBench/main/leaderboard.csv) are public. These benchmarks measure different capabilities: perfect character recognition does not guarantee correct tables or reading order.

## What are the best open-source OCR engines?

Traditional OCR engines recognize printed text and work well on clean scans. They tend to be straightforward to deploy, although many need another component for structured output.

### PaddleOCR: open-source OCR engine

PaddleOCR is Baidu's Apache-2.0 OCR toolkit. Its PP-OCR pipeline combines text detection and recognition, supports multilingual text and runs on CPUs or GPUs. In independent testing, PP-OCRv6 scored **71.9% mean text accuracy**, processed **48 pages per minute** on an L4 host and cost approximately **$0.06 per 1,000 pages** in compute. It is a strong starting point for custom OCR pipelines, though complex document structure may require PP-Structure or other postprocessing. See [LlamaParse vs PaddleOCR](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-paddleocr).

### Tesseract: simple OCR without a GPU

Tesseract remains useful for printed text in scanned documents. It is free, Apache-2.0 licensed and runs on CPUs. In independent testing, it reached **67.8% mean accuracy** and **36 pages per minute** on the reference host, but only **43.9% handwriting accuracy**. Pair it with OCRmyPDF to make scanned PDFs searchable. It is not a complete solution for reconstructing complex tables or charts. See [LlamaParse vs Tesseract](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-tesseract-ocr).

### EasyOCR: quick Python OCR projects

EasyOCR is an Apache-2.0 PyTorch library supporting 80+ languages. It returns text, bounding boxes and confidence scores through a straightforward Python interface. Independent testing measured **59.6% mean accuracy**, **20 pages per minute** and around **$0.15 per 1,000 pages** in compute. It is easy to prototype with, but trails newer document-focused models for parsing complex PDFs. See [LlamaParse vs EasyOCR](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-easyocr).

### docTR: customizable OCR pipelines

docTR combines text detection and recognition with structured geometry for pages, blocks, lines and words. It works well for teams building custom downstream processing. Its independent results were **67.1% mean accuracy**, **34 pages per minute** and approximately **$0.08 per 1,000 pages** in compute. It is Apache-2.0 licensed, but document interpretation beyond text and geometry remains the developer's responsibility. See [LlamaParse vs docTR](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-doctr).

## Which open-weight OCR models are best for document parsing?

Document vision-language models can produce Markdown or structured output while preserving more of the layout than traditional text recognition.

### PaddleOCR-VL: fast, low-cost local parsing

PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 is a compact document vision-language model for text, tables, formulas and layouts. It scores **50.90 on ParseBench**, including **50.62 on charts**; a visual grounding score of 8.78 pulls its overall result down. Independent testing found **73 pages per minute** on an L4 at about **$0.04 per 1,000 pages** in compute. It also reports **96.34 on OmniDocBench v1.6**. Different benchmark results underline the importance of testing on your actual document types.

### Surya: local OCR with layout detection

Surya, developed by Datalab, provides OCR, reading order, layout analysis and table recognition. Surya OCR 2 scores **60.63 on ParseBench**, including **82.74 on tables** but **19.04 on charts**. Independent testing measured **18 pages per minute** on an L4 and around **$0.16 per 1,000 pages**. Datalab also develops Marker and Chandra. **Check model-weight licensing:** Surya's code is Apache-2.0, but its weights have extra commercial restrictions.

### MinerU: self-hosted PDF conversion

MinerU is an option for teams that want to run model-based PDF conversion locally and produce Markdown or JSON. MinerU2.5-Pro scores **69.27 on ParseBench**, with **77.61 on tables**, **59.12 on charts** and **74.24 on visual grounding**. It is worth considering when local execution and document structure matter more than a lightweight text-only pipeline. Its exact version lacks a comparable independent speed-and-cost run. The repository's license adds commercial thresholds and attribution requirements, so review its current terms before deploying it as a service.

### olmOCR: raw text and handwriting accuracy

olmOCR from Allen AI focuses on faithful PDF transcription. In independent testing, olmOCR 2 achieved **94.3% mean accuracy**, including **97.4% on handwriting**, at **18 pages per minute** on an L4 and around **$0.16 per 1,000 pages** in compute. It has no ParseBench score yet, so test it separately on complex page structure and charts.

### Docling: flexible, local document conversion

Docling is an MIT-licensed document conversion toolkit supporting PDFs and Office documents with Markdown, HTML and structured JSON output. It integrates OCR engines and table recognition in configurable pipelines. The public ParseBench Docling-models configuration scores **50.65**, including **52.76 on charts**. The leaderboard marks this run unverified because its published outputs are incomplete, so treat its 1.03 semantic-formatting score with caution. See [LlamaParse vs Docling](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-docling).

## What are the best cloud OCR APIs?

Cloud services avoid the work of hosting models, but differ in document structure, pricing tiers and downstream processing needs.

### Google Document AI: OCR inside Google Cloud

Google Document AI provides OCR, form extraction and layout processing. Enterprise Document OCR starts at **$1.50 per 1,000 pages**, while Layout Parser is **$10 per 1,000 pages**. The Layout Parser configuration scored **48.66 on ParseBench**, including **54.95 on tables** and **1.59 on charts**. Google Cloud integration is a procurement consideration. Compare its named processor with LlamaParse on the documents and outputs required by the application. See [LlamaParse vs Document AI](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-document-ai).

### Azure AI Document Intelligence: Microsoft-based workflows

Azure AI Document Intelligence extracts text, tables, selection marks and layouts, with Markdown support in Layout. Azure Layout scores **56.76 on ParseBench** and **85.97 on tables**, the strongest table result among the three hyperscaler APIs here, while its chart score is **1.27**. Layout is billed per 1,000 pages; see [Azure's regional pricing](https://azure.microsoft.com/en-us/pricing/details/document-intelligence/) for the current rate. Existing Microsoft infrastructure is a reason to include Azure in a trial, not evidence that it delivers better document results than LlamaParse. See [LlamaParse vs Azure Document Intelligence](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-azure-document-intelligence).

### Amazon Textract: forms and tables in AWS

Amazon Textract extracts text, handwriting, tables and form data through AWS APIs. Basic text detection starts at **$1.50 per 1,000 pages**, and table analysis at **$15 per 1,000 pages**. ParseBench measured Textract at the $15 table-analysis price, where it scores **48.31 overall**, with a much stronger **84.46 on tables** but **4.47 on charts** and **4.65 on semantic formatting**. It is useful for AWS-native forms and table workloads, although complex RAG pipelines may need postprocessing. See [LlamaParse vs Amazon Textract](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-amazon-textract).

### Mistral OCR: affordable managed Markdown extraction

Mistral OCR converts documents into Markdown, including tables and other content. The benchmarked OCR 4 configuration scores **58.38 on ParseBench**, increasing to **68.23 with annotations** (unverified). Current [OCR 4.1 pricing](https://docs.mistral.ai/models/ocr-4-1) is **$4 per 1,000 pages**, or **$5 per 1,000 annotated pages**. The table reports the older OCR 4 benchmark configuration and its recorded cost separately; its score is not a measurement of OCR 4.1.

## Can GPT or Gemini replace a dedicated OCR model?

General-purpose multimodal models can read PDFs, but costs change with output length and reasoning budgets.

### Gemini: PDF understanding through a general-purpose model API

Gemini supports PDF inputs and structured responses. Gemini 3 Flash with high thinking scores **73.98 on ParseBench** at a measured **$24.10 per 1,000 pages**. Minimal thinking gives **72.47** at **$6.50 per 1,000 pages**, within two points of GPT-5.6 Sol at about a twelfth of the cost. On the full leaderboard, the top general-purpose model is Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort, at 78.80. Gemini can be a good choice when reading documents is part of a broader reasoning task. At scale, variable token and thinking costs require attention.

### GPT: OCR within a broader reasoning task

OpenAI GPT models can process PDFs and generate extracted text or structured output. GPT-5.6 Sol with high reasoning scores **74.40 on ParseBench**, at a measured **$80.80 per 1,000 pages**. GPT-6.1 Terra with medium reasoning scores **73.64** (unverified) at **$10.90 per 1,000 pages**. Terra scores **93.07 on tables** but **52.94 on visual grounding**. Dedicated parsers can be more economical for repeated large-scale parsing.

## What about desktop OCR software?

### ABBYY FineReader: desktop document conversion

ABBYY FineReader provides OCR and PDF conversion for desktop and enterprise workflows, including export to Word and Excel. [FineReader PDF Corporate](https://pdf.abbyy.com/pricing/) is **$165 per year**, with a Hot Folder batch limit of 5,000 pages a month. There is no public ParseBench score for it in this comparison, and subscription pricing is not directly comparable to API per-page costs. It is primarily suited to human-led document conversion. See [LlamaParse vs ABBYY FineReader](https://www.llamaindex.ai/compare/llamaparse-vs-abby-finereader).

## Which OCR model should you choose?

| Goal or constraint | Recommendation | What to validate |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Best overall production document processing | LlamaParse | Parsing quality, extraction accuracy, source evidence and deployment |
| Insurance packets, invoices and financial reports | LlamaParse with Extract | Complete records, document identity and business-rule checks |
| Complex tables, charts and cross-page context | LlamaParse Agentic Plus | Source labels, units, missing rows and citations |
| Optimize processing cost while retaining quality | LlamaParse Agentic or Cost Effective | Accepted outputs and total operating cost by tier |
| Open-source local parser required | LiteParse; compare local alternatives | Dependencies, output requirements and operating responsibility |
| Handwriting-only recognition | olmOCR 2 or PaddleOCR-VL; test your own samples | Accuracy on your languages and handwriting styles |
| Human-led conversion to Word or Excel | ABBYY FineReader | Export quality and page limits |
| Customer-cloud or on-prem processing | LlamaParse Enterprise | Exact model, network and regional configuration |

A model can recognize every character in a filing but lose the relationship between a table header and its numbers. Another might recognize chart labels without preserving the chart's data. For extraction, retrieval and agents, those errors matter more than a character-level OCR score alone.

## Frequently asked questions about OCR models

### What is the best OCR model in 2026?

For production documents, LlamaParse. Agentic Plus scores **86.69 on ParseBench**, the highest overall score in this comparison, and Agentic scores **82.83 at $12.50 per 1,000 pages**. For text-only scans, start with LiteParse, which is free and runs locally.

### Which OCR handles tables and charts best?

Among dedicated parsers and OCR tools, LlamaParse Agentic Plus leads on both: **93.27 on tables** and **92.19 on charts**, the highest chart score on the ParseBench leaderboard. Cloud OCR APIs do well on tables but recover almost no chart data: Azure Layout scores 85.97 on tables and 1.27 on charts, and Amazon Textract scores 84.46 and 4.47. Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort scores 94.26 on tables but 70.89 on charts.

### What is the best free OCR?

For PDFs, LiteParse. It is LlamaIndex's Apache 2.0 parser: it runs locally with no API key, reads scanned pages, and rebuilds headings, tables and lists into Markdown, or returns JSON with bounding boxes. For dense tables, charts and difficult scans, use LlamaParse.

### Which OCR tools run offline?

LiteParse, Tesseract, PaddleOCR, EasyOCR, docTR, PaddleOCR-VL, Surya, MinerU, olmOCR and Docling all run locally once installed. Check the licenses for Surya and MinerU before commercial use. For harder documents, LlamaParse Enterprise runs air-gapped on the Cost Effective and Agentic tiers when OCRia runs on your own GPUs.

### Can GPT or Gemini replace OCR?

For a few documents, yes. At volume, a dedicated parser scores higher for less. LlamaParse Agentic scores **82.83 at $12.50 per 1,000 pages**. GPT-5.6 Sol scores 74.40 at $80.80 and Gemini 3 Flash scores 73.98 at $24.10. The best general-purpose model, Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort, scores 78.80 at $61.30.

### Is Tesseract still good enough in 2026?

For clean printed text, yes. It is free, runs on a CPU, and scored 67.8% mean accuracy at 36 pages per minute in independent testing. It scored 43.9% on handwriting and does not rebuild tables or charts.

### Which OCR model handles handwriting best?

Among the tools in this guide, olmOCR 2 scored highest in an independent 22-engine test, at **97.4%**, followed by PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 at **95.8%**. Test your own samples: one handwriting set does not cover every language or historical document.

### What's the difference between OCR and document parsing?

OCR turns pixels into text. Document parsing also keeps reading order, tables, headings and chart values, so downstream systems can use the document. A model can read every character in a filing and still attach a number to the wrong column header.

## Try LlamaParse on your documents

If your PDFs contain complicated tables, charts or layouts, [try LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse) on your files. The free plan includes **10,000 credits per month**. Review the [ParseBench leaderboard](https://www.parsebench.ai/) or [start with the API docs](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/).

# Chandra vs LlamaParse for Chart Extraction: Accuracy, Units and Source Evidence

LlamaParse Agentic Plus has the higher chart score in the published ParseBench comparison with Chandra OCR 2. That matters when an analyst needs numbers, series and units rather than a figure description. Start with that measured advantage, then check whether printed values, visual estimates and footnotes survive the complete application workflow.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Product facts reflect research through October 28, 2026. Examples below are hypothetical, not measured vendor outputs.*

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 93.27 | 92.19 | 75.43 |
| Chandra-ocr-2 | 70.59 | 89.20 | 62.77 | 51.18 |
| Datalab Accurate | 72.88 | 90.66 | 63.20 | 51.38 |

Agentic Plus scores 92.19 on charts, versus 62.77 for Chandra OCR 2 and 63.20 for Datalab Accurate. This supports prioritizing LlamaParse for a chart-heavy trial. It does not imply that Datalab cannot extract chart values or that every visual estimate will be exact.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## What does Chandra return for charts?

Chandra 2.5 introduced a consistent figure representation containing fields for alternative text, visible text, axes, data, diagram structure and description. Its announcement says chart values estimated from an axis are marked with `~`. These capabilities followed chart understanding in earlier releases; chart extraction should not be portrayed as missing from Datalab. [Chandra 2.5 release](https://www.datalab.to/blog/chandra-2-5), [Chandra 1.5 release](https://api.datalab.to/blog/chandra-1-5).

Those fields give downstream code predictable places to look for chart data. The harder integration work starts when a value reaches a spreadsheet: which year does it describe, what are its units, and was it printed or estimated? An approximation that works for a chart summary may be unsuitable for an accounting reconciliation.

## Printed numbers, visual estimates and calculations

Separate three categories before designing a score:

| Value category | What the document provides | Appropriate evaluation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Printed value | A visible numeric label | Transcription and association accuracy |
| Axis-derived estimate | Position relative to a scale | Error tolerance appropriate to resolution and scale |
| Derived quantity | A value calculated from other values | Correct inputs, formula and explanation |

Keep the category with each extracted value so a downstream model can tell a published number from a visual approximation.

A useful output record includes the value, unit, series, period, page and a description of its evidence. When the value was estimated, retain that status rather than stripping it during normalization. When the source is ambiguous, uncertainty is preferable to unsupported precision.

## Worked example: a regional revenue chart

Imagine a hypothetical chart titled “Revenue by region, \$ millions.” It shows North America and Europe for 2024 and 2025. One bar has a printed label of 120; another has no label and appears close to 95 on the axis.

An extraction system could produce a neat table containing 120 and 95. That table still needs several checks. Does 120 belong to North America or Europe? Is 95 explicitly estimated? Has “millions” been preserved? Are the values for a fiscal year or a calendar year? Does a footnote say that 2024 was restated?

For the unlabeled bar, a suitable record might say “approximately 95 million,” linked to the chart’s page. For the printed label, the record should preserve 120 without inventing extra decimal places. If the footnote changes comparability, retain it alongside the values rather than leaving it in unrelated page text.

## How should chart extraction be scored fairly?

Start with the intended use. A chart used for search may need a faithful description and preserved image. A chart used for numerical analysis needs correctly associated values. A chart used for audited reporting may require printed evidence rather than estimates.

Then define a scoring policy before reviewing outputs:

1. Score printed numeric labels separately from visual estimates.
2. Accept equivalent table orientations and sensible series names.
3. Check units, multipliers and negative values independently.
4. Distinguish missing values from invented values.
5. Record whether chart images and source locations remain accessible.
6. Count document failures and incomplete charts, not only returned cells.

Datalab has publicly questioned aspects of ParseBench’s chart-estimation and formatting methodology. Investigating those vendor criticisms requires checking the disputed cases and scoring rules. In particular, does the score reflect the application’s needs, and are equivalent valid outputs treated consistently? [Datalab’s ParseBench critique](https://www.datalab.to/blog/why-we-built-omniparsebench).

For ParseBench, that means making the rubric, examples and accepted normalizations available for scrutiny, including cases raised by competitors.

## Which documents belong in a chart test set?

Include more than clean vertical bar charts. A practical test set should cover stacked bars, multiple axes, line charts, small multiples, negative values, crowded legends and figures with explanatory footnotes.

Stratify by source quality as well. A vector PDF, a low-resolution scan and a screenshot can contain the same chart but present very different evidence. Preserve the original input type in the test manifest instead of averaging those cases without explanation.

Use examples that represent business risk. For financial analysis, incorrect units may matter more than a stylistic description. For scientific search, omitting a confidence interval may change the interpretation. For operational dashboards, associating a series with the wrong region can be more damaging than a small visual estimation error.

Report these errors beside the average. An analyst needs to know whether the remaining mistakes concern small visual estimates or the units used in a financial model.

## Putting the chart output into an application

LlamaParse’s published chart-score advantage provides the reason to evaluate it first for numerical chart output. Inspect estimate markers, units and source evidence throughout the application, including transformations after parsing. Datalab’s structured figure output is a capability to test against that contract, not a substitute for the measured comparison.

Start with LlamaParse Agentic Plus for the chart-heavy evaluation, using its measured ParseBench advantage as the shortlist evidence. Then test the ten charts that feed an actual decision, including printed values, estimates, units and footnotes. Measure downstream answer correctness separately from the parsing score.

title: "Reducto vs LlamaExtract Grounding: Evidence Accuracy Behind Extracted Fields"
description: "LlamaExtract Agentic Plus leads Reducto Deep Extract on word-level grounding in the standard ExtractBench snapshot, even though their overall Value F1 scores are close."
published: "2026-10-22"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/"
---

# Reducto vs LlamaExtract Grounding: Evidence Accuracy Behind Extracted Fields

LlamaExtract Agentic Plus leads Reducto Deep Extract on word-level grounding in the standard ExtractBench snapshot, even though their overall Value F1 scores are close. That is a meaningful distinction for audit workflows. Evaluate whether the cited passage supports the correct entity, year and unit, as well as whether a citation exists.

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on ExtractBench

| Configuration | Value F1 | Long-document Value F1 | Word grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 96.17 | 94.65 | 83.25 |
| Reducto Deep Extract | 96.08 | 92.85 | 50.76 |

Agentic Plus records 83.25 word-grounding F1 versus 50.76 for Reducto Deep Extract, a 32.49-point difference. Overall Value F1 is nearly tied. That makes localized supporting evidence a more specific reason to evaluate LlamaExtract than a claim of a large average value-accuracy lead.

These are published results from the pinned ExtractBench snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026. The suite covers 370 documents and 4,869 pages. Value F1 measures extracted values; it is not a straight-through-processing rate. LlamaIndex publishes the benchmark and develops LlamaExtract, now documented within LlamaParse Extract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench.md).

## Reducto’s citation output

Reducto's extraction citations can include page locations, bounding boxes and source text, with separate parse and extract confidence signals. The documentation permits empty citation arrays when a value is inferred or its source cannot be localized. It also notes that enabling extraction citations disables chunking. These are relevant configuration details for an evidence-oriented evaluation. [Reducto extraction citations](https://docs.reducto.ai/configs/extract/citations)

Reducto also documents word- and cell-level locations for parsed content. Parsing locations and evidence attached to a particular extracted field serve related but different purposes: a field review must establish which source material supports that field's meaning. [Word and cell citations](https://docs.reducto.ai/configs/parse/citations)

The buyer's question is therefore more specific than whether the API offers bounding boxes. It is whether the evidence is sufficient for the decision the application is about to make.

## Give reviewers more than “citation present”

Use an explicit evidence taxonomy. A directly stated value can be checked against a visible source span. A calculated value may require several inputs and a documented transformation. An inferred value needs a different review policy because no single source span necessarily states the answer.

| Evidence state | Suggested review treatment |
| --- | --- |
| Directly supported | Verify the cited span and field interpretation |
| Calculated from supported inputs | Inspect inputs and calculation |
| Inferred from context | Apply an inference-specific approval policy |
| Localization unresolved | Request better evidence or manual inspection |
| Unsupported or contradictory | Block automatic acceptance |

These are proposed application states, not a claim that every vendor emits these labels. The application can derive them through validation and review. Preserve the provider's raw response so the added interpretation remains auditable.

## Include the heading, unit and surrounding clause

A bounding box can point to a real number while failing to establish its role. Financial tables may contain the same amount in different periods or units. A reviewer needs the associated row label, column heading and any relevant footnote to decide whether the field was interpreted correctly.

Similarly, an address can be correctly located but belong to a billing party rather than a beneficiary. Evidence localization and semantic attribution should therefore be scored separately. A location score should not conceal a wrong-field error.

When designing a viewer, display enough surrounding context to support the judgment. Cropping too tightly can remove the very heading that makes a value meaningful. Keep a route back to the full page for ambiguous cases.

## A monthly payment and an annualized estimate

In a hypothetical lease review, the output lists a monthly payment of \$2,000 and an annual payment of \$24,000. The source states only the monthly amount; the annual amount is calculated by multiplication. This is an illustrative scenario, not a result from either provider.

The monthly value can have direct evidence. The annual value should identify the monthly input and the calculation, rather than pretending the source explicitly states \$24,000. If the lease includes a free month or an escalation clause, the simple calculation may be inappropriate even though the arithmetic is correct.

A reviewer should be able to see the payment clause, the term and any exception affecting the annualized amount. The acceptance policy may allow a clearly labeled estimate for analysis while prohibiting it as a contractual obligation.

The annualized payment needs an explanation of its calculation and assumptions. A direct citation alone cannot provide that explanation.

## Calibrate confidence against review decisions

Treat confidence as an input to a decision policy, not a substitute for evidence. Before adopting a threshold, inspect labeled examples across the score range. Ask whether lower-confidence fields actually require more correction and whether high-confidence errors remain.

Use different thresholds for different consequences if the workload warrants it. An uncertain optional description and an uncertain bank-account number should not necessarily trigger the same response. Track the resulting false accepts and unnecessary escalations.

A comparison between providers must not assume their numeric confidence scales are interchangeable. Evaluate the decisions produced by each calibrated policy on the same held-out documents. Report the policy alongside the results so another team can understand the tradeoff.

## Audit the fields that drive the decision

Reducto’s page, text and bounding-box evidence can support a useful review interface. The next question is how well that evidence lets a reviewer resolve a particular field. Start with fields that control a payment, approval or contractual interpretation, and label value correctness separately from evidence sufficiency.

The published grounding comparison above supplies evidence for LlamaExtract’s localized-evidence advantage. The field-level audit described here is a separate application test; no new reviewer-time study is reported. Include inferred values and unresolved locations in that audit.

## Can confidence scores be compared across vendors?

Only with calibration evidence. The same numeric score need not mean the same error rate in two systems. Compare the acceptance decisions each policy produces on labeled documents, then examine high-confidence errors and unnecessary escalations. A review threshold is useful when it controls those outcomes, not simply because it looks precise.

Evaluate LlamaExtract Agentic Plus first when localized source evidence is central to the workflow, using its word-grounding advantage rather than overstating the small overall value-score difference. Include years, units and entity labels in the evidence audit. Measure production review outcomes separately.

title: "Extend Light and Performance vs LlamaParse: Accuracy, Routing and Cost"

# Extend Light and Performance vs LlamaParse: Accuracy, Routing and Cost

LlamaParse offers a measured quality advantage over the tested Extend Light and 2.0 configurations on ParseBench. Start with those results, then choose the least expensive configuration that meets your difficult-document requirements. Extend Auto’s routing is a separate workflow choice; an engine’s low page rate is useful only when its output passes the application’s quality floor.

*Published by LlamaIndex. This guide explains a selection method; it does not claim measured savings or a newly tested accuracy ranking.*

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic | 82.83 | 90.90 | 81.20 | 69.42 |
| LlamaParse Cost Effective | 77.68 | 86.72 | 73.98 | 62.22 |
| Extend (2.0) | 73.50 | 85.26 | 76.02 | 69.79 |
| Extend Light (1.0) | 71.26 | 75.74 | 75.99 | 69.64 |

Agentic scores 82.83 overall, compared with 73.50 for Extend 2.0 and 71.26 for Extend Light 1.0. Cost Effective also has a higher overall score than those Extend rows, but Extend is slightly ahead of Cost Effective on charts and visual grounding. Choose the LlamaParse tier around the content you need to preserve; these rows do not evaluate Extend Auto routing.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## What do the three Extend parsing options do?

Extend describes Performance as its accuracy-oriented parser, Light as a faster and cheaper option with limitations on harder content, and Auto as per-page difficulty routing. The documented Light weaknesses include difficult scans, handwriting, large tables, non-Latin languages and dense checkbox regions. [Parsing configuration](https://docs.extend.ai/parsing/configuration).

Pull examples of those difficult page types into the test set, even if they make up little of the monthly volume.

Keep parsing separate from extraction in the comparison. A statement about Parse Light is not evidence about the behavior of an extraction engine with a similar name. Record the product layer and configuration explicitly.

## Why can average accuracy give the wrong answer?

Imagine a hypothetical corpus with 9,500 clean digital pages and 500 difficult scanned pages. A configuration could do very well on the first group while failing requirements on the second. The weighted average might still look attractive.

If the difficult pages contain the documents that trigger regulatory review, their small volume does not make their errors unimportant. A procurement decision based only on the weighted average can select the wrong operating point for the business.

Use two views together:

| View | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Volume-weighted result | What outcome should we expect across normal traffic? |
| Per-stratum result | Which document groups meet or miss their requirements? |
| Critical-case result | Do rare, high-consequence documents remain safe to use? |
| Accepted-output cost | What do usable results cost after repair and review? |

Use the weighted result for capacity planning and the subgroup results to decide which pages need review or a different route.

## How should you define a quality floor?

Write an acceptance rule for each important output. A search application may require correct titles, text and table associations. A form-processing application may require every checkbox state and its label to remain connected.

Then define which failures can be repaired automatically, which require review and which should reject the document. A missing decorative image may be acceptable. A missing negative sign in a financial figure may not be.

Avoid choosing a threshold merely because a vendor clears it. Start with downstream consequences and label examples of acceptable and unacceptable outputs. This gives evaluators a consistent reference when a result is technically valid but operationally unhelpful.

Apply the same thresholds to LlamaIndex configurations. If every checkbox must retain its label, keep that requirement fixed across the comparison.

## How do you test adaptive routing fairly?

An adaptive system should be judged on the results and total work produced by its routing policy. Record the document mix, actual charges, output quality and completion time. Where available, preserve routing or effective-configuration information for diagnosis.

Do not compare a carefully tuned adaptive setup with an untuned static baseline and attribute every difference to the architecture. Give each candidate a reasonable development phase, then freeze settings before the holdout test.

Also test distribution changes. A system selected on mostly clean pages may behave differently when the next batch contains more scans. Run a sensitivity analysis by changing the proportions of document groups without changing the scoring rules.

## What would a practical evaluation look like?

Start with a small labeled sample from each important group. For example, define separate sets for clean forms, poor scans, dense tables and mixed-language documents. These are proposed test categories, not a claim about a particular customer's files.

Run each eligible configuration on the same inputs. For every result, record whether it passed the acceptance rule, what repair was needed and how long it took to become usable. Keep the unmodified output for later inspection.

Next, investigate failures rather than immediately averaging them. Were fields omitted? Were relationships lost? Was the output accurate but inconvenient for the downstream application? Different failure types suggest different remedies.

Set a re-test trigger before deployment: a new supplier family, a higher scan share, a version change or a sustained rise in review. Save the original group-level results so the team can see what changed.

## Make the quality-cost tradeoff explicit

Extend's choices are useful when a team wants explicit options for cost-sensitive ingestion, harder pages or mixed-complexity routing. Its credit documentation distinguishes their billing, which should be included in a configuration-specific budget. [How credits work](https://docs.extend.ai/general/how-credits-work).

Compare the least expensive qualifying Extend configuration with the least expensive qualifying LlamaIndex configuration. Include repair work in that calculation. A rate difference is easier to interpret once both options meet the application's requirements.

The fair conclusion may be different for different workloads. Some teams will prefer one engine everywhere for simplicity. Others will accept routing complexity to improve their quality-cost balance.

## Pull out the difficult minority first

Use LlamaParse Agentic as the quality-led starting point for mixed documents, then test cheaper tiers against explicit quality floors. Keep Extend Light, Performance and Auto results separate. Select the least expensive configuration that actually passes on the difficult minority rather than averaging those failures away.

# Best Document AI for Insurance Claims and Underwriting: Evaluating LlamaParse

**Our first recommendation for insurance teams building document-processing workflows is LlamaParse.** Evaluate it for claims packets, underwriting submissions, schedules and supporting financial records. Its parsing and extraction capabilities address the document work behind those processes, while a standalone API lets the team retain its existing claims or policy application.

The purchase should be based on accurate, complete information with traceable sources. The recommendation does not depend on building a RAG chatbot or adopting the LlamaIndex framework.

## What does an insurance workflow need from a document platform?

A claims upload can contain several business documents, each with different fields and context. A policy identifier on an early page may apply to a later schedule. An amended value may supersede an earlier one. Repeated invoices must stay attached to the correct claim and supplier.

A useful processing layer should help the application identify documents, preserve boundaries and extract the records required by the next operational step. LlamaIndex describes insurance document-agent use cases; qualify the specific implementation against your own packet types. [Insurance overview](https://www.llamaindex.ai/industry/insurance).

## How would LlamaParse fit a claims packet?

Consider a hypothetical property-claim packet containing a claim form, repair invoices, a schedule and an assessor’s report.

A proposed implementation can use the following path:

| Stage | Processing choice | Required acceptance check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identify the incoming type | Classify with document-type rules | Correct type and explicit handling of unknown material |
| Separate bundled PDFs | Split where the packet requires it | Correct page groups and no lost attachments |
| Preserve document content | Parse | Tables, headings, units and page identity retained |
| Produce required records | Extract with the target schema | Correct fields, complete repeated items and source evidence |
| Apply the operational policy | Existing application and review process | Missing information and contradictions escalated |

Classify and Split are documented APIs. Split is beta and subject to breaking changes; test its behavior before relying on it in a production intake route. [Classify](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/classify/), [Split](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/split/).

This describes an architecture to implement. It does not claim that a parser independently decides coverage, authorizes payments or supplies a complete claims-management system.

## What supports choosing LlamaParse for difficult insurance documents?

The pinned ParseBench results place LlamaParse Agentic Plus at 86.69 overall, including 93.27 on tables and 92.19 on charts. ParseBench includes enterprise pages from domains such as insurance and finance. Those are parsing results across the benchmark, not a dedicated claims-processing accuracy percentage. [ParseBench results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv).

For difficult extraction, the pinned Pro snapshot records 77.70 Value F1 and 38% perfect documents for LlamaExtract Agentic Plus, compared with 56.35 and 3% for the Reducto Deep row. That supports evaluating LlamaParse on the difficult-document workload itself. Pro is a synthetic long-tail suite, not an insurance-specific adjudication study. [Pro results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv).

LlamaIndex publishes these benchmarks and develops the products. Pair the public evidence with an insurance-specific acceptance set.

## What should the underwriting trial include?

Use representative submissions and the cases that cause rework: continued schedules, missing pages, handwritten additions, amended terms and documents containing more than one entity.

Define which values should be extracted, which should remain unresolved and what source is authoritative when documents disagree. For repeated schedules, score every required row rather than only a few header fields.

Keep human operational decisions separate from document output. A correctly extracted amount can still require context or approval before the business acts on it.

## Can the platform fit an existing insurance system?

Yes: use the API as the document-processing layer and pass accepted records into the system already used by the team. The framework used to orchestrate that application is optional.

LlamaParse also documents managed, single-tenant, BYOC and on-premises options. Review the exact configuration, contracts and data flows for the proposed workload; the deployment label alone does not establish the necessary controls. [Deployment documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/general/enterprise-readiness/deployment/).

## How should the team choose?

Start with LlamaParse as the overall document-processing candidate. Measure complete records, evidence quality, packet identity, review effort and cost per accepted document.

Include an alternative when it satisfies a requirement worth testing, but do not treat a competitor’s insurance page, review interface or existing cloud integration as an accuracy result. Make the selection on the information the team can reliably use in claims and underwriting work.

# LlamaParse vs GPT, Claude and Gemini for PDF parsing (2026)

*Disclosure: LlamaIndex makes LlamaParse and built ParseBench. LlamaParse combines its own models, including OCRia-1, with models from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. This comparison uses published ParseBench results, with evaluation code and outputs available through the benchmark repository.*

**Is LlamaParse better than sending PDFs straight to GPT, Claude or Gemini?** On the published ParseBench comparison, LlamaParse Agentic leads the tested general-purpose configurations overall: 82.83 at \$12.50 per 1,000 pages, versus 78.80 at \$61.30 for Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort. That supports evaluating it first for complex document parsing. For a few simple PDFs and a one-off answer, a direct model call can be enough.

- **Best overall:** LlamaParse Agentic Plus, 86.69
- **Best value for complex PDFs:** LlamaParse Agentic, 82.83 at \$12.50 per 1,000 pages
- **Tables:** Claude Opus 5.5 at high effort leads, 94.26 vs 93.27 for Agentic Plus
- **Charts:** LlamaParse Agentic Plus leads, 92.19 vs 70.89 for Opus
- **Lowest cost shown:** GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning and Claude Haiku 5.5, \$1.40 per 1,000 pages, scoring 61.03 and 56.02
- **Bounding boxes and page confidence:** returned by LlamaParse; frontier models give coordinates only when prompted

## Which LlamaParse advantages matter for a buying decision?

The clearest supported case is the tested combination of overall parsing quality, chart interpretation and localized evidence. Agentic Plus leads the tested high-effort Opus row on charts by 21.30 points (92.19 versus 70.89) and visual grounding by 14.87 points (75.43 versus 60.56). Opus leads on tables (94.26 versus 93.27) and content faithfulness (91.25 versus 89.74), so a table-only claim would tell a different story. [Pinned ParseBench results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv).

Use those differences to choose what to trial first. The benchmark tests the specified parsing prompts and configurations; it does not establish that LlamaParse wins every question-answering task or every custom model pipeline.

## How do GPT, Claude, Gemini and LlamaParse compare?

These are published [ParseBench results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv) at leaderboard commit 0ccc167 (November 2, 2026). Scores are on a 0–100 scale. Overall is the mean of five dimensions: tables, charts, content faithfulness, semantic formatting and visual grounding. It is a benchmark score, not the percentage of documents parsed without errors.

| Setup | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding | Cost per 1,000 pages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | **86.69** | 93.27 | **92.19** | **75.43** | \$56.25 |
| LlamaParse Agentic | 82.83 | 90.90 | 81.20 | 69.42 | \$12.50 |
| LlamaParse Cost Effective | 77.68 | 86.72 | 73.98 | 62.22 | \$3.75 |
| Claude Opus 5.5, high effort | 78.80 | **94.26** | 70.89 | 60.56 | \$61.30 |
| Claude Opus 5.5, default | 76.97 | 93.88 | 64.12 | 58.44 | \$57.90 |
| Claude Haiku 5.5 | 56.02 | 86.85 | 10.13 | 27.63 | \$1.40 |
| GPT-6 Astra, low reasoning | 69.81 | 93.18 | 35.08 | 56.04 | \$98.70 |
| GPT-6 Luna, medium reasoning | 61.03 | 86.76 | 42.97 | 29.60 | \$1.40 |
| GPT-6 Luna, max reasoning | 64.13 | 87.44 | 45.71 | 41.48 | \$7.20 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash, low thinking | 69.15 | 88.22 | 35.12 | 67.81 | \$7.10 |
| Gemini 3.8 Flash, high thinking | 71.20 | 89.15 | 32.58 | 69.03 | \$34.10 |
| Google Cloud Document AI | 48.66 | 54.95 | 1.59 | 61.26 | \$10.00 |

Costs convert the leaderboard's cents per page into dollars per 1,000 pages. They describe the benchmark workload and configurations, excluding downstream model calls and optional processing features. Token-based costs will vary with your documents and current provider rates. The table covers the published configurations listed here, not every current model; no speed ranking is claimed.

**Our recommendation:** start with LlamaParse Agentic for mixed PDFs. It scores 4.03 points above Opus at high effort for about one-fifth of the parsing cost. Use Agentic Plus when chart extraction is a priority. If tables dominate your workload, test Opus alongside it: Opus has the strongest table result here. For the lowest processing spend among the displayed setups, GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning and Haiku 5.5 both cost \$1.40 per 1,000 pages, with lower overall scores.

## How were these PDF parsing results measured?

[ParseBench](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench) covers approximately 2,000 human-verified pages from enterprise documents, including insurance, finance and government material. The comparison uses published, verified leaderboard rows; the [pipeline definitions](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/main/docs/pipelines.md) specify each model and reasoning configuration. The frontier-model file pipelines process individual pages as native PDFs and use detailed instructions for Markdown, HTML tables, chart data and layout coordinates, with the full layout prompt available in the [source code](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/main/src/parse_bench/inference/providers/parse/_layout_utils.py). The repository links evaluation code and published outputs; these results measure page parsing, not whole-document question answering or every possible custom pipeline.

## Where do the differences show up?

### Charts need the underlying values, not just a description

A model can describe a chart correctly while failing to recover its data. If your agent compares quarterly revenue, it needs values associated with the right series, dates and units. A readable paragraph about the trend will not do that job.

Charts show a large gap in these results. Agentic Plus scores 92.19, compared with 70.89 for Opus at high effort, 35.08 for GPT-6 Astra at low reasoning and 32.58 for Gemini 3.8 Flash at high thinking. Even Cost Effective, at 73.98, exceeds those three model configurations on this dimension.

That makes chart-heavy financial reports a strong reason to evaluate a parser before committing to direct model calls. It does not mean every chart fails with a frontier model. It means the aggregate results favor LlamaParse on this task.

### Tables are a real strength of frontier models

Merged headers and spanning cells determine which value belongs to which category. Flatten a two-row header incorrectly and a number can end up attached to the wrong year or business unit, even when every character was transcribed correctly.

Opus at high effort scores 94.26 on tables, ahead of Agentic Plus at 93.27. GPT-6 Astra also performs strongly at 93.18, above Agentic's 90.90. A dedicated parser does not automatically win every document task.

If you mostly process tables, compare the actual structures each setup returns. Check merged cells, repeated headers and missing rows alongside cost. The overall leaderboard alone should not decide a table-only workload.

### Reading text and preserving the page are different tasks

Dense reports combine paragraphs, footnotes, figures and multiple columns. A pipeline can recover the words while losing the relationship between them. That matters when a footnote changes the meaning of a value or a heading determines which section a paragraph belongs to.

ParseBench scores content faithfulness and semantic formatting separately for this reason. Opus at high effort exceeds Agentic Plus on content faithfulness, 91.25 versus 89.74. LlamaParse leads on semantic formatting: Agentic scores 84.81 and Agentic Plus 82.84, versus 77.06 for Opus. The useful question is which errors would break your workflow: missing text, lost structure, incorrect chart values or misplaced source regions.

## When is sending a PDF directly to a model enough?

Start with a direct model call when you have a small number of readable PDFs, straightforward layouts and a specific question to answer. Summarizing a short report or finding a clause may not require a reusable parse of every page. Existing API integration also makes this a practical starting point. Check a representative sample, including the hardest pages, before expanding the workflow. Add a parsing layer when you need consistent document output across many files, reliable chart data or source regions for review. Volume matters, but so does the cost of a quiet error in a single document.

## What do you build yourself with direct model calls?

The initial request can be simple. Keeping it reliable across changing documents takes more work:

- **Page handling:** split oversized files, preserve page identity and reassemble results in order.
- **Retries and throughput:** handle rate limits, transient errors, concurrency and partial failures without duplicating work.
- **Incomplete output:** detect truncation, missing sections and refusals, then decide what to retry or review.
- **Output checks:** enforce the expected structure and validate values against your business rules. Schema-valid JSON can still contain incorrect values.
- **Grounding:** connect text, tables and values to source pages and regions your users can inspect.
- **Quality assessment:** decide which results need review and evaluate that decision on your own documents.
- **Cost control:** track input, output and reasoning usage, then retest when prompts or models change.

LlamaParse provides a maintained parsing API and structured document output. Your team still owns downstream business validation and the decisions made from that output. For the longer engineering discussion, see [LLM APIs Aren't Complete Document Parsers](https://www.llamaindex.ai/blog/llm-apis-are-not-complete-document-parsers).

## How does each model API handle PDFs?

### Gemini

[Gemini's document-processing API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/document-processing) supports native PDF understanding, including text and visual content, with documented limits of 50 MB or 1,000 pages. Gemini 3.8 Flash at low thinking costs \$7.10 per 1,000 benchmark pages and scores 69.15 overall. High thinking raises the overall score to 71.20 and cost to \$34.10, but does not improve every category. Its 69.03 visual-grounding score exceeds LlamaParse Cost Effective (62.22) and nearly matches Agentic (69.42), though Agentic Plus leads at 75.43. That is a reason to test its prompted coordinates, alongside its lower chart scores, rather than assume a parser always locates content more accurately.

### GPT

[OpenAI's PDF input support](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/pdf-files) supplies extracted text and page images to compatible vision models. GPT-6 Astra at low reasoning performs well on tables, scoring 93.18, but scores 69.81 overall at \$98.70 per 1,000 benchmark pages. Luna offers a cheaper starting point: medium reasoning costs \$1.40 with a 61.03 overall score. Increasing Luna to max reasoning raises that score to 64.13 and cost to \$7.20. Choose the model and reasoning setting together, then measure whether the extra spend improves the content your workflow actually needs.

### Claude

[Claude supports PDF text and visual analysis](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/pdf-support). Opus 5.5 at high effort is the strongest verified general-purpose model setup overall in this leaderboard snapshot and the table leader in this comparison, at \$61.30 per 1,000 pages. Claude also offers [native PDF page citations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations), so citations alone are not a reason to add a parser. Page citations and bounding boxes serve different needs: one identifies the page supporting an answer; the other identifies a region within it. Haiku 5.5 is substantially cheaper here, with a lower overall score of 56.02.

## Can you get bounding boxes and confidence scores?

Yes, but distinguish the output interface from its measured accuracy.

LlamaParse returns [structured bounding boxes](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/features/layout-and-bounding-boxes/), with options for word, line and table-cell grounding. Frontier models can also generate coordinates when prompted; ParseBench explicitly asks them to do so. Gemini's visual-grounding result, above LlamaParse Cost Effective and close to Agentic, shows why “native output” and “most accurate boxes” should be evaluated separately.

LlamaParse also exposes page confidence in its [result metadata](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/guides/response-format/). Its optional high-effort assessment adds document-level confidence and a breakdown for an additional five credits per page, equivalent to \$6.25 per 1,000 pages at the documented credit rate. A number a model generates after being asked “how confident are you?” should not be treated as a calibrated probability of correctness. Validate review thresholds against labeled examples from your own workload.

## Frequently asked questions

### Can Gemini replace OCR?

Gemini can read text and visual content from PDFs, including pages that require visual recognition. For a direct question or summary, that can be sufficient. Test completeness, table structure and chart values before using it to replace the parsing stage of a production workflow.

### Is GPT good at reading tables in PDFs?

Yes. GPT-6 Astra at low reasoning scores 93.18 on ParseBench tables, close to Agentic Plus at 93.27. Its lower chart and overall scores show why table performance should not be generalized to every PDF task.

### Does LlamaParse use GPT, Claude or Gemini?

LlamaParse uses its own models, including OCRia-1, and models from those providers within a maintained parsing pipeline. You can send its output to GPT, Claude or Gemini afterward. Using LlamaParse does not require choosing the LlamaIndex framework for the rest of your stack.

### What does parsing 1,000 pages cost?

In this benchmark snapshot, LlamaParse costs \$3.75 on Cost Effective, \$12.50 on Agentic and \$56.25 on Agentic Plus. Direct model costs range from \$1.40 for the displayed Luna and Haiku configurations to \$98.70 for Astra. These are parsing costs; optional features and subsequent reasoning or extraction calls add to the total.

### How do I turn contracts or invoices into JSON?

Parsing preserves document content and structure. Extracting invoice totals or contract renewal terms adds a field schema and task-specific checks. Use schema-guided extraction, such as LlamaParse Extract, or build that step on parsed content with your chosen model. ParseBench measures parsing and does not establish field-extraction accuracy.

[Try LlamaParse](https://www.llamaindex.ai/pricing) with 10,000 free credits per month and compare its output with your current model on the same documents.
