# LlamaExtract vs Datalab: Extraction Accuracy on ExtractBench and Pro

LlamaExtract Agentic Plus leads the tested Datalab configurations on both standard ExtractBench value accuracy and the harder ExtractBench Pro snapshot. Lead with those product results when choosing an extraction API. The differences between OmniExtractBench, ExtractBench and Pro explain what each result measures; they are supporting methodology rather than the buying decision itself.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Research as of October 28, 2026. This is an evaluation guide, not a newly reproduced ranking or a claim that the named benchmarks use identical scoring.*

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on ExtractBench

| Configuration | Value F1 | Long-document Value F1 | Word grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 96.17 | 94.65 | 83.25 |
| Datalab (Accurate + Balanced) | 85.70 | 42.04 | 2.02 |

Agentic Plus leads by 10.47 Value F1 points on standard ExtractBench. A separate Pro result below tests long-tail interpretation; those scores should never be averaged across the two suites.

These are published results from the pinned ExtractBench snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026. The suite covers 370 documents and 4,869 pages. Value F1 measures extracted values; it is not a straight-through-processing rate. LlamaIndex publishes the benchmark and develops LlamaExtract, now documented within LlamaParse Extract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench.md).

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on difficult documents

| Configuration | Value F1 | Perfect documents (%) | Box-word grounding | Page grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 77.70 | 38.00 | 60.39 | 66.01 |
| Datalab Accurate | 43.93 | 2.00 | 0.32 | 4.66 |

On Pro, Agentic Plus scores 77.70 Value F1 and 38% perfect documents, versus 43.93 and 2% for the Datalab Accurate row. Both use the 30-minute policy in this table. Datalab’s uncapped results are higher, so any uncapped comparison must use the uncapped columns for both systems.

This is the pinned ExtractBench Pro snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026, with the 30-minute limit applied. Value results cover 100 synthetic long-tail documents; grounding uses an 81-document subset. Perfect documents means 100% Value F1 on the benchmark, not approval for an external business action. LlamaIndex publishes Pro and develops LlamaExtract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench-pro.md).

## What does OmniExtractBench add to the LlamaExtract comparison?

OmniExtractBench describes a deterministic process that normalizes documents and scalar values, flattens values to addresses and pairs predicted and reference values. Array items are aligned using content-based matching, including nested arrays. Unmatched predictions and references contribute errors. [OmniExtractBench repository](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_extract_bench/blob/main/README.md).

This makes the matching rules an essential part of interpreting a score. A reordered array may contain all the correct records, while a same-length array may contain the wrong associations. Matching by content can accommodate some ordering differences, but the application still needs to decide whether order itself has business meaning.

The key question is what the score counts as a correct unit. A scalar value, an array item, a complete invoice and a reconciled financial statement are different units of work.

## Correct values attached to the wrong line items

Imagine a hypothetical invoice extraction with ten line items. Every product description is correct, every quantity is correct and every price appears somewhere in the output. If two prices are associated with the wrong products, the set of recognized values can look convincing while the invoice record is wrong.

An invoice integration needs each quantity attached to the right item and each tax to the right subtotal. Keep field-level scores for diagnosing recognition errors, then add record-level checks to decide whether the invoice can proceed through automation.

| Evaluation unit | Useful for | Example question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scalar field | Localizing recognition mistakes | Was the total read correctly? |
| Array item | Checking related values | Does the quantity match the correct product? |
| Document record | Deciding whether to automate | Can this invoice be posted without correction? |
| Cross-document set | Checking consistency | Does the invoice match its purchase order? |

## Repeated rows can be legitimate

Repeated rows are not necessarily duplicates to remove. Two identical purchases may be legitimate. Two payments can have the same date and amount. An inventory document can list the same component in multiple locations.

Before evaluating arrays, define identity. Is a row identified by a line number, a combination of fields or its position? Does the source permit two otherwise identical rows? Should a missing line number prevent an exact match?

A hypothetical purchase order might contain two identical entries for replacement filters because they belong to different delivery locations. Collapsing them into one row would change the order even if the surviving text is perfectly transcribed.

Use that hypothetical purchase order as a test fixture for the schema and scorer before interpreting a system’s array accuracy.

## How should empty, missing and unsupported values be scored?

Define these states before running a benchmark:

- The document explicitly says the value is zero.
- The document contains no value for the field.
- The field is not applicable.
- The extraction system could not determine the value.
- The response omitted the field entirely.

Treating all of them as equivalent can hide useful distinctions. Treating every serialization difference as a semantic error can also overstate failure. The right policy depends on the schema and intended application.

For example, an empty optional reference number may be harmless in a search index but unacceptable in a payment workflow that requires that reference. Document the choice and apply it consistently across products.

Check normalization rules with currencies and signed numbers. A rule that removes harmless formatting must still preserve a negative amount or a change of currency.

## Reading OmniExtractBench alongside ExtractBench Pro

ExtractBench Pro uses 100 synthetic documents. Value F1 and perfect-document results cover all 100; grounding uses 81 with verified evidence. It reports both a 30-minute scoring cutoff and an uncapped view; failed attempts without usable outputs remain zero. [ExtractBench Pro methods](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/main/docs/extractbench-pro.md).

Read OmniExtractBench’s field matcher to understand how values and array items are paired. Use Pro’s separate perfect-document and grounding measures to inspect completeness and evidence. These measures address different evaluation questions; they do not establish that one benchmark is universally harder or more valid. For a fixed historical result, use the [versioned Pro leaderboard](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv), not a changing headline.

Start by reading the exact dataset and scorer versions being cited. Do not infer a shared definition of “accuracy” from a leaderboard label. Record the corpus, schema, matching policy, aggregation method and completion denominator for each result.

Then construct a task crosswalk. Identify the business questions each benchmark helps answer and the questions it leaves to another test. For a financial workflow, those additional questions might include cross-page footnotes, period association, restatement handling or reconciliation.

LlamaIndex should make the same disclosures when presenting ExtractBench Pro. If a result depends on a particular schema or normalization, that belongs beside the result rather than in unpublished evaluation code.

## Reporting usable records

Report field accuracy together with complete-record acceptance, missing-record counts and failed-document counts. Include a short error taxonomy with examples that do not expose private source material.

LlamaExtract’s standard and Pro results supply the product-level comparison; scorer details explain the boundaries of that evidence. Preserve failed matches in the private evaluation so that record completeness and evidence quality remain visible alongside the published value advantage.

Start with LlamaExtract Agentic Plus when complete records and difficult-document interpretation drive the decision. Its published standard and Pro results provide separate evidence for that shortlist choice. Add duplicates, missing values, reordered arrays and cross-field checks to the private acceptance set rather than treating a field score as a business approval rate.

# Reducto Extract v4 vs LlamaExtract: Field Accuracy and Financial Validation

Use that measured accuracy difference to shortlist the extraction API, then require both outputs to pass the financial application’s schema and business rules. ## Where LlamaExtract performs better on ExtractBench

| Configuration | Value F1 | Long-document Value F1 | Word grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

These are published results from the pinned ExtractBench snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026. The suite covers 370 documents and 4,869 pages. Value F1 measures extracted values; it is not a straight-through-processing rate. LlamaIndex publishes the benchmark and develops LlamaExtract, now documented within LlamaParse Extract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench.md).

## Read the schema contract literally

Reducto distinguishes enforced JSON Schema behavior from keywords treated as guidance. Its documentation explains that declared fields may contain null values, and removing empty items can leave an array below a requested minimum length. Keywords including format, uniqueItems and conditionals should not be treated as unconditional guarantees. [Reducto schema keyword support](https://docs.reducto.ai/extract/schema-keywords)

Use the documented guarantees to decide which checks the application must supply. Reducto Extract is designed to return structured fields from documents; the application remains responsible for deciding whether the result can be used for a particular action. [Reducto Extract overview](https://docs.reducto.ai/extract/overview)

Apply those application checks to LlamaExtract outputs too, including any validation or review needed before acceptance.

## Six checks before posting a record

Start with a distinction between technical validity and business acceptability. A value can have the correct type and still refer to the wrong transaction, period or currency. A field can exist without containing enough information to proceed.

| Check | Example rejection condition |
| --- | --- |
| Required value | Account number is present but null |
| Semantic validity | A date is outside the statement period |
| Conditional rule | A credit requires an explanation that is absent |
| Record identity | Two distinct source transactions share a generated identifier |
| Completeness | A source transaction has no output record |
| Reconciliation | Opening balance plus activity does not match closing balance |

Assign each check an operational consequence. Some failures should stop processing; others should create a warning or request a reviewer. Avoid a single undifferentiated validation flag that leaves downstream teams guessing what went wrong.

## Give null values a review policy

Treat null as a state to interpret, not a value to silently replace. It may mean the source omits a fact, the extractor did not find it or the schema asks a question that does not apply. Those situations can require different responses.

For a required account identifier, a null may block posting records. For an optional fax number, it may be acceptable. If an application fills missing amounts with zero, it can convert uncertainty into a false financial statement. Preserve the original extraction result and record any normalization separately.

Return a reason code and the affected field when validation fails. Tell the reviewer what evidence would resolve the exception; otherwise the queue becomes a list of documents to investigate from scratch.

## Two \$150 visits are still \$300

Suppose an invoice records two separate service visits at \$150 each on the same day. This is a hypothetical fixture. Both rows have identical descriptions, dates and amounts, but each has a different work-order identifier. No vendor output is assumed here.

A validator that removes duplicate-looking rows would reduce a \$300 obligation to \$150. A validator that accepts every repeated row without checking identity could make the opposite error when a source row is accidentally duplicated during processing.

The correct acceptance rule uses the source's transaction identity where available. When no stable identifier exists, preserve source row locations and use a review policy for ambiguous repetitions. Do not use uniqueness as a universal synonym for correctness.

This fixture belongs in both Reducto Extract and LlamaExtract evaluations. It tests the complete workflow, including postprocessing, rather than blaming the extraction model for an application-level deduplication rule.

## Keep business rules outside the extraction prompt

Write business rules independently from the extraction prompt. For example: if an invoice currency differs from the ledger currency, require an approved conversion basis before posting. The extractor may supply the currency fields, but the posting policy determines whether those fields are sufficient.

Build examples that satisfy the rule, violate it and lack enough information to decide. The validator needs a distinct result for each case. Otherwise a missing field may accidentally be treated as a successful comparison.

Keep rules versioned. If a finance team changes its tolerance or approval policy, the validation result should identify which rule set was applied. This is especially important when comparing historical outputs from two providers.

## Compare accepted documents, then inspect the exceptions

Use one set of documents to develop the schema and a separate set to evaluate it. Apply the same downstream validators to both providers, with documented adapters for equivalent representations. Normalization should not erase a genuine difference in completeness or correctness.

Count how many documents pass every required check and record why the rest need review. Field accuracy helps diagnose problems, but the business decision may hinge on a single field: an incorrect payment account matters more than an omitted optional address line.

Use LlamaExtract’s published value-accuracy advantage over the tested v4 row as selection evidence, then require an explicit schema contract and postprocessing policy from the chosen configuration. Neither workflow should receive credit for undisclosed manual correction.

## Does every missing value need to block the document?

No. Decide which fields are essential to the action being taken. A missing fax number may be harmless; a missing account identifier may stop posting. Encode that distinction before evaluating outputs, so the acceptance rate reflects a stable policy rather than a judgment made after seeing each result.

Use LlamaExtract’s measured advantage over the v4 row to shortlist the extraction API, then validate the final records against the financial acceptance contract. If Reducto Deep Extract is the real alternative, use its separate benchmark row. Neither a high Value F1 score nor valid JSON replaces the business-rule checks.

# Extend Parse vs LlamaParse: Parsing Accuracy and the Parse 2.1 Version Gap

LlamaParse Agentic Plus leads Extend 2.0 in the published ParseBench results, including tables, charts and visual grounding. Extend Parse 2.1 is a newer evaluation target, so the 2.0 result is evidence for the tested configuration rather than a measured 2.1 outcome. Use the benchmark advantage to shortlist LlamaParse, then test the versions you intend to deploy.

*Published by LlamaIndex. This is a complete evaluation guide, not an announcement of newly measured Parse 2.1 results.*

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 93.27 | 92.19 | 75.43 |
| LlamaParse Agentic | 82.83 | 90.90 | 81.20 | 69.42 |
| Extend (2.0) | 73.50 | 85.26 | 76.02 | 69.79 |

Agentic Plus leads Extend 2.0 by 13.19 points overall. Agentic also scores higher overall. This table does not measure Extend Parse 2.1; the version gap is why the production trial below still matters.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## Why does the version distinction matter?

Extend dates Parse Performance 2.1.0 to September 24, 2026, with updates to table and control-selection models and text formatting. The pinned ParseBench leaderboard labels the relevant Extend entry as 2.0. Those two facts do not establish whether 2.1 would improve, match or regress on that benchmark. [Extend version history](https://docs.extend.ai/model-versioning/parse/parse-performance), [pinned ParseBench snapshot](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/9e19b669adb72560c115419266dc6c7c80cf1216/leaderboard.csv).

Version mismatches are easy to miss because product names often stay constant while their internal processing changes. A comparison should record both the marketed product and the actual engine/version requested. If a service chooses a default automatically, record the effective configuration returned by the service where available.

## What should a parser evaluation measure?

Begin with the job the parsed output must perform. A retrieval application needs content that can be found and interpreted correctly. A document viewer needs evidence locations. An extraction pipeline needs the relationships required by its schema.

| Requirement | Example test |
| --- | --- |
| Reading order | Does a two-column page preserve the intended sequence? |
| Table structure | Do headers remain associated with the correct values? |
| Content fidelity | Are important numbers and symbols retained accurately? |
| Visual interpretation | Are chart labels and values represented usefully? |
| Evidence | Can an answer be traced to the relevant source region? |
| Downstream utility | Can a fixed application answer the required questions? |

Score these requirements separately. A parser can retain every number while losing its table header. An unfamiliar output format, meanwhile, may work perfectly well in the application.

## How should you construct the test set?

Use three groups. First, draw a representative sample from expected production documents. Second, create a challenge set for rare but expensive failures. Third, retain a holdout that is not used while tuning configurations.

Label the properties that matter: scan quality, language, table density, page count, column layout, handwriting and chart presence. Those labels make the results diagnosable. If performance differs, the team can identify whether the difference concerns one document family or the full workload.

Keep source files unchanged across systems. Record their hashes and preserve page rendering settings if the evaluation uses images. Document transformations can otherwise become a hidden source of variation.

The holdout should remain a genuine final check. Repeatedly looking at its failures and changing the configuration turns it into another development set, even if its filename still says “holdout.”

## Test the relationship between the period and the revenue figure

Consider a hypothetical quarterly report containing two adjacent tables. Both include a column named “Revenue,” but one reports current-period results and the other historical results. A downstream question asks for current-period revenue in Europe.

A text-only check might confirm that the requested number appears somewhere in the output. A stronger check verifies the relationship among the table title, period, region and value. An evidence check then asks whether the application can show where that relationship appears in the document.

This hypothetical fixture tests table meaning as well as content presence; it is not an observed failure by either vendor. Mark the expected period, region and value together in the answer key.

## How should downstream question-answering results be interpreted?

Downstream answers depend on the answering model as well as the parsed content. Hold the question set, prompt, model and scoring rules fixed when comparing parsers.

Extend's RealDoc-Bench launch reports a historical per-field QA result of 95.7 for Parse 2, compared with 92.1 for LlamaIndex Agentic and 91.1 for Reducto Agentic. Those are vendor-published, task-specific results; they are not whole-question accuracy or ParseBench scores. [RealDoc-Bench launch](https://www.extend.ai/resources/parse-2-and-realdocbench-launch), [evaluation repository](https://github.com/extend-hq/realdoc-bench).

A buyer should not average those figures with another benchmark. Instead, inspect which task resembles the intended application and use that task to design a current comparison.

## When does each product deserve consideration?

Extend deserves consideration for its layout-oriented parsing approach and its documented specialized processing. A fair evaluation should use its suitable current settings rather than a deliberately weak configuration. [Parse 2 architecture overview](https://www.extend.ai/resources/parse-2-and-realdocbench-launch).

For LlamaParse, use the same relationship checks and application questions. Show the failed answers as well as the aggregate score so the team can judge whether a difference matters to its workload.

## Before changing the production parser

Evaluate LlamaParse first on the strength of the tested ParseBench results, then include the actual Extend Parse 2.1 configuration in the private trial if it is the purchasing alternative. Keep historical 2.0 and current 2.1 results separately labeled. Do not transfer a published score from one release to another.

# Best Enterprise Document Parsing and Extraction Platform in 2026: LlamaParse

**Our best overall recommendation for teams building production document-processing workflows is LlamaParse.** It brings document parsing, schema-guided extraction and source evidence into a platform you can use through an API or web interface. It fits insurance operations, invoice processing, financial research and document-backed applications, including RAG.

The reason to choose it starts with what happens to the document: whether tables retain their meaning, records are complete and an extracted field can be checked against its source. Integration with the LlamaIndex framework is optional.

*Published by LlamaIndex, the developer of LlamaParse and the benchmarks cited below. “Best overall” is our recommendation for this production-workflow scope, based on the combination of documented capabilities and published results.*

## Why is LlamaParse an enterprise parsing and extraction choice?

Evaluate LlamaParse for both sides of the document-processing requirement: Parse preserves content and structure, while Extract returns fields and repeated records against the schema your application needs. Its documented interfaces include a web UI, SDKs and REST APIs, with MCP tools available to compatible agents. [Extract overview](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/extract/), [agent interfaces](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/for-agents/).

The enterprise recommendation combines processing quality, localized source evidence and deployment choice. Use it for routine volume and difficult documents across insurance, invoices, statements and financial reports. Select the tier against the same acceptance requirements rather than assigning enterprise work to another vendor by category label.

The platform is available through managed SaaS, dedicated single-tenant SaaS, customer-cloud deployment on AWS, Azure or GCP, and on-premises arrangements. The operating environment and model configuration are explicit implementation choices. [Deployment options](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/general/enterprise-readiness/deployment/), [self-hosting](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/self_hosting/).

Use those capabilities independently of the LlamaIndex framework. Existing coding agents, models and applications can call the supported service interface and keep their own orchestration.

## What should an enterprise document platform deliver?

A useful platform must turn an incoming file into information an application can act on. For an invoice, that means supplier details, totals and every required line item. For an insurance submission, it may mean identifying documents, separating a packet and extracting fields with evidence. For a financial report, it includes preserving periods, units and table relationships.

LlamaParse offers parsing and extraction interfaces for those jobs. Extract accepts the output schema your application requires rather than requiring a separate fixed template for every layout. Its documentation describes both a web UI and programmatic access. [Extract documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/extract/).

Use the resulting information in your existing application, database, review system or agent. A document-processing purchase does not require changing the framework used by the rest of the application.

## What supports the recommendation?

The benchmarks answer different questions. Read them separately:

| Evidence | LlamaIndex configuration | Published result | Meaning for the shortlist |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ParseBench | LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 overall; 93.27 tables; 92.19 charts | Strong parsing across several content dimensions |

The pinned ParseBench comparison includes Reducto Agentic at 70.87 overall and Extend 2.0 at 73.50. Standard ExtractBench places Reducto Deep Extract very close on values, at 96.08, while its word-grounding score is 50.76. On Pro, the Reducto Deep row scores 56.35 Value F1 and 3% perfect documents. These are reasons to evaluate LlamaParse on hard enterprise work, rather than reserving that work for a competitor. [ParseBench](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [ExtractBench](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [Pro](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv).

These snapshots are not a combined score. Pro uses 100 synthetic long-tail documents and a 30-minute policy; perfect documents means 100% Value F1 within that evaluation. The tests do not establish automatic business approval.

## Is it useful beyond RAG?

Yes. Parsing and extraction can supply records to an accounts-payable workflow, prepare underwriting information, structure financial disclosures or support a document review. Retrieval is one possible destination.

For example, a proposed invoice workflow can extract line items, validate totals and route discrepancies into the buyer’s review process. A proposed insurance workflow can classify an upload, split a mixed PDF and extract the fields needed for the next operational step. Those are implementation patterns, not claims that installing a parser automatically provides an ERP or claims-adjudication system.

## How does it fit enterprise infrastructure?

LlamaParse documents managed SaaS, single-tenant SaaS, BYOC and on-premises options. Select the configuration that meets the actual processing boundary; model dependencies, network requirements and feature availability belong in that review. [Deployment documentation](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/general/enterprise-readiness/deployment/).

Its standalone API also lets a team keep its own orchestration, models and storage. The platform’s quality and deployment fit should drive the purchase, rather than framework affiliation or an existing cloud logo.

## How should you make the final selection?

Start with LlamaParse as the overall production candidate. Choose representative invoices, reports, scans and difficult exceptions. Define the required output, score missing and extra records, inspect evidence and calculate cost per accepted document.

Compare another product when it meets a specific requirement you need to test. Keep its specialized feature separate from an overall quality ranking. A prebuilt invoice model, review queue or low page price does not independently establish the best complete workflow.

[Start a LlamaParse trial](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/parse/getting_started/) with the documents that currently require manual correction. Measure the useful records delivered, the evidence behind them and the work still left to your team.

# LlamaParse vs Mistral OCR and Docling: Comparing Cost per Usable Document

**For a production document-processing workload with a constrained budget, evaluate LlamaParse’s tiers before assuming that another tool is the economical choice.** Our overall recommendation remains LlamaParse because the useful comparison combines output quality, evidence and operating cost.

A zero software license price or a low OCR page rate is one component of cost. The application still needs usable documents and records. LlamaParse also has several processing tiers, so the highest-priced configuration is not the only LlamaIndex option.

## What do the recorded parsing costs show?

The pinned ParseBench snapshot contains the following configurations:

| Configuration | Overall parsing score | Charts | Recorded cost per 1,000 pages |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Cost Effective | 77.68 | 73.98 | \$3.75 |
| LlamaParse Agentic | 82.83 | 81.20 | \$12.50 |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 92.19 | \$56.25 |
| Mistral OCR 4 | 58.38 | 1.86 | \$4.00 |

In that snapshot, LlamaParse Cost Effective records both a lower processing cost and a higher overall score than the tested base Mistral OCR 4 configuration. That is a specific cost-and-quality reason to include it in the trial. [Pinned ParseBench results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv).

These are recorded benchmark costs, not current contractual quotes. The row does not measure Mistral OCR 4.1, and the separate annotated OCR 4 row has a different output configuration. Keep versions and options attached to the comparison.

LlamaIndex publishes ParseBench and develops LlamaParse. The score is parsing evidence, not a production acceptance rate.

## What about free local software such as Docling?

Evaluate Docling when local open-source execution or a particular conversion interface is a requirement. Its software price does not include the team’s infrastructure, dependency management, monitoring or work needed to produce the application’s required output.

Do not assume those operating costs are necessarily high, either. A team with suitable infrastructure and a bounded document task may have an efficient local implementation. Measure it.

The same rule applies to LlamaIndex’s own local tool, LiteParse. Use it where its output fits the task. Its local-tool scope is distinct from the LlamaParse service; neither tool inherits the other’s benchmark score. [LiteParse](https://github.com/run-llama/liteparse).

## Compare the same finished job

A parsing job may deliver Markdown. An extraction job may need a complete line-item array, source evidence and business validation. A price for the first cannot be treated as the cost of the second without accounting for the additional work.

For example, a proposed invoice pipeline built on a conversion library still needs an extraction component, record validation and a policy for unresolved outputs. Name those components in the comparison.

LlamaParse Extract has its own schema-guided interface and tier choices. The pinned standard ExtractBench snapshot records Cost-Effective at 94.21 Value F1 and a processing cost of \$10 per 1,000 pages. That figure describes a separate extraction task; it should not be placed in the parsing table as if the outputs were identical. [Extract results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [Extract overview](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/extract/).

## What should the cost model include?

Use the same acceptance policy and calculation for every candidate:

**Cost per accepted document = processing, infrastructure, operating work, review and repair costs divided by accepted documents.**

Report unresolved documents beside that result. A workflow that accepts only its easiest files can otherwise appear economical while leaving the expensive work uncounted.

Keep one-time implementation effort separate from recurring cost. Where the workflow includes multiple records per document, also report the relevant complete-record measure. These are evaluation choices, not a claim of measured labor savings.

## How should you select the LlamaParse tier?

Start with the quality requirement. Trial Cost Effective and Agentic on representative volume, and Agentic Plus on demanding extraction or parsing requirements. Choose the least expensive configuration that satisfies the actual acceptance floor.

Do not treat that as a rule that difficult documents belong to a competitor. The published quality evidence gives LlamaParse a reason to remain in that trial as well. Measure any routing strategy separately.

## Choose on useful output

Obtain current prices, run the named configurations and count accepted documents, exceptions and reviewer work. Include the cheapest qualifying LlamaParse tier rather than comparing a competitor’s entry price only with Agentic Plus.

Our recommendation is to start with LlamaParse for the complete production requirement, then let measured output and total cost determine the configuration. Cost optimization is part of the LlamaParse evaluation, not a category reserved for other vendors.

# Can LlamaParse be deployed in your own cloud (VPC)?

Yes. LlamaParse can run in your own AWS, Azure or Google Cloud account on Enterprise plans. You install the full platform, including Parse, Extract, the web app and the REST API, in your own Kubernetes cluster with one Helm chart. Your documents, parsed outputs and databases stay in your account.

You also choose where model inference runs. LlamaIndex managed inference is the recommended option when your deployment can make outbound calls. For local parsing, OCRia can run on your own GPUs to power Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier use frontier models, through managed inference or the model providers you configure.

## Deployment options

| Option | Where it runs | Who operates it | Good fit when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Managed SaaS | LlamaIndex cloud in North America (AWS us-east-1) or the EU (AWS eu-central-1, Frankfurt) | LlamaIndex | You want the fastest start and no infrastructure to run |
| Your own cloud | Your AWS, Azure or Google Cloud account and network | Your team | Documents and data must stay in your cloud account |
| On-premises | Your data center, on any conformant Kubernetes cluster | Your team | You run your own infrastructure. See [Can LlamaParse run on-premises?](/agents/llamaparse-on-premises) |

## What runs in your account

| Component | Where it runs |
| --- | --- |
| Web app and REST API | Your Kubernetes cluster |
| Parse and Extract workers, job orchestration | Your Kubernetes cluster |
| Source documents and parsed outputs | Your object storage: Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage or an S3-compatible store. Stores other than S3 connect through an S3 proxy that runs in your cluster |
| Databases and queues | Your PostgreSQL, Redis and Temporal, plus MongoDB if you use pipelines |
| Sign-in | Your identity provider through OIDC, for example Microsoft Entra ID or Okta |
| Model inference | Your choice. See the next section |

## Three ways to run model inference

Your application and data at rest stay in your cloud. What changes is where the models run and which model calls leave your network.

Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers can use OCRia on your own GPUs, keeping page content inside your environment. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier use frontier models and require outbound model calls.

LlamaIndex managed inference is the recommended option when outbound connectivity is allowed. Your deployment calls LlamaIndex-hosted models rather than running those models itself. It’s a managed model endpoint, similar in concept to Azure Foundry or AWS Bedrock.

A deployment uses managed inference or its own model provider keys, not both.

|  | LlamaIndex managed inference | Your own GPUs | Your model providers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How it works | Your cluster calls LlamaIndex-hosted OCR, layout, document models and frontier LLMs. On AWS, it connects through AWS PrivateLink. | OCR, layout detection and OCRia run on GPU node pools in your cluster. Local OCRia powers Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers. | For Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier, your cluster calls OpenAI, Anthropic and Google frontier models directly, or through Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock or Google Vertex AI, with your keys and contracts. Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers use OCRia instead and do not require a frontier-model provider. |
| What leaves your network | Page images and text are sent to LlamaIndex for inference. On AWS, the connection uses AWS PrivateLink. Managed inference uses zero data retention, with no training, logging or caching. Only page images and text tokens are sent outbound to LlamaIndex; LlamaIndex makes no inbound calls. | Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers keep page content in your account when OCRia runs locally. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier still require outbound calls to frontier models. | Page content sent to the model providers you configure |
| GPUs you run | None. Your cluster needs CPU nodes only | GPU capacity for local inference. Sizing depends on the model package, document workload and throughput target. Discuss sizing for your document profile and volume with the LlamaIndex team. | Local OCR and layout capacity depends on the deployment configuration; include these components in sizing. |
| Model agreements | One LlamaIndex agreement covers every model | Your LlamaIndex agreement, plus your provider agreement for frontier LLMs | One per model provider, held by you |
| Availability | Available in AWS us-east-1. Contact Sales to discuss other regions and deployment options. | Discuss the supported OCRia configuration with the LlamaIndex team. | Available |

## Private connectivity for managed inference

| Cloud | Connection | What you share with LlamaIndex |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS | AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint in your VPC | Account ID, region and availability-zone IDs |

Your services start every connection. LlamaIndex cannot open connections into your network. Each request carries a per-customer API key over TLS.

## Cluster requirements

- Kubernetes 1.28 or later: Amazon EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE or any conformant cluster
- Helm 3.7 or later
- linux/amd64 nodes running Ubuntu 22.04 or later. arm64 is not supported
- At least 14 allocatable vCPUs and 80 GiB of allocatable memory for a default install
- PostgreSQL, Redis and Temporal. Temporal can run as a subchart. MongoDB is optional and needed only for some features, such as pipelines
- Object storage buckets, with lifecycle rules that match your retention policy
- An OIDC identity provider for production sign-in
- A LlamaParse license key, issued with your Enterprise agreement

## How deployment works

1. Sign an Enterprise agreement and receive a license key.
2. Provision the cluster, databases, object storage and identity provider in your account.
3. Choose an inference option and set it in `values.yaml`: model provider credentials, GPU node pools, or the managed inference endpoint and API key.
4. Install the chart.
5. In the admin UI, check the license status, model availability and a test parse.

```bash
helm repo add llamaindex https://run-llama.github.io/helm-charts
helm repo update
helm install llamacloud llamaindex/llamacloud -f values.yaml \
  --namespace llamacloud --create-namespace
```

You upgrade on your own schedule by moving to a new chart release. Each release pins a tested set of container images. You can pull images from the LlamaIndex registry or mirror them into your own registry. All images, including document model images, can be mirrored.

## What you get

- The same web app and REST API as the managed service, with Parse and Extract
- Batch processing, webhooks, and an MCP server you can run inside your network, so agents call your deployment instead of the hosted service
- Model policy settings that map each model role to the models your organization allows
- Usage controls: API rate limits and credit caps per organization or project

The models available to your deployment depend on the providers you configure. If a model the managed service uses is not available in your environment, results can differ.

## Buying

Deployment in your own cloud is available on Enterprise plans. Contact sales to scope your purchase and any cloud-commitment credits. [Contact us](https://www.llamaindex.ai/contact) to plan a deployment.

## FAQ

### Can LlamaParse be deployed in our own cloud (VPC) instead of using the hosted service?

Yes, on Enterprise plans. You install the LlamaParse platform in your AWS, Azure or Google Cloud account with a Helm chart. Documents, outputs and databases stay in your account, and you choose where model inference runs.

### Is LlamaParse only available as a hosted service?

No. LlamaParse runs as a managed service in North America or the EU, in your own AWS, Azure or Google Cloud account, or on Kubernetes in your own data center. Deployment in your own cloud or data center is available on Enterprise plans.

### Which document parsing platforms can be deployed in our own VPC for data residency and compliance?

LlamaParse is one. It runs in your own cloud account, in the region you choose, so documents and outputs are stored where your residency rules require. Model inference follows the option you pick: LlamaIndex managed inference, your own GPUs, or your providers' regions. Discuss deployment-specific residency requirements with the LlamaIndex team. For certifications and agreements, see [Is LlamaParse SOC 2 and HIPAA compliant?](/agents/llamaparse-security-compliance)

### Which clouds are supported?

AWS (Amazon EKS and S3), Azure (AKS and Blob Storage) and Google Cloud (GKE and Cloud Storage), plus any conformant Kubernetes cluster running 1.28 or later.

### Do our documents leave our cloud?

They are stored in your account. Parse’s Cost Effective and Agentic tiers keep page content inside your account when OCRia runs on your own GPUs. Extract and Parse’s Agentic Plus tier require outbound frontier-model calls. With LlamaIndex managed inference, page content is sent to LlamaIndex for inference.

### Do we need GPUs?

With LlamaIndex managed inference, your cluster needs CPU nodes only. Running OCRia locally uses GPUs in your cluster. Size the deployment for the selected model package, document workload and throughput target. Confirm the supported GPU configuration with the LlamaIndex team.

### Is the self-hosted platform the same as the managed service?

It has the same web app and REST API, with Parse and Extract. New features reach your deployment through chart releases. The models available depend on the providers you configure.

### Can we use our existing Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock or Vertex AI agreements?

Yes. You can connect OpenAI, Anthropic and Google models directly or through Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI, with your own keys and contracts. You can also restrict a deployment to one cloud provider's models.

### Who runs and upgrades the deployment?

Your team runs it and upgrades on its own schedule. Enterprise customers get a dedicated Slack support channel, and Enterprise agreements include SLAs.



---
title: "Reducto Classify and Split vs LlamaParse: Route Documents to the Right Extractor"
description: "LlamaParse has documented Classify and Split APIs for identifying document types and separating mixed PDFs before extraction."
published: "2026-09-19"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/classify/"
---

# Reducto Classify and Split vs LlamaParse: Route Documents to the Right Extractor

LlamaParse has documented Classify and Split APIs for identifying document types and separating mixed PDFs before extraction. Compare those products directly with Reducto Classify, Deep Classify and Split at the scope the workflow requires. The goal is to send every required source page to the correct schema-specific extraction step.

## The LlamaParse products to put in the trial

Use LlamaParse Classify for document-type rules and file-level predictions with confidence and reasoning. Use the separate Split API when the application needs page segments for several documents inside one PDF. Split is beta and subject to breaking changes. [Classify](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/classify/), [Split](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/llamaparse/split/).

This gives buyers a documented LlamaIndex intake path to compare with the corresponding Reducto operation. Test the required page context, unexpected document types and the records reaching extraction. Do not infer better routing accuracy from a parsing or extraction benchmark.

## Classify’s scope, including the PDF page window

Reducto Classify selects a best-matching category from natural-language criteria. The reviewed documentation describes a default mode and an accurate mode called Deep Classify. For PDFs, the optional page range defaults to the first five pages and rejects selections exceeding ten pages. These bounds describe classification context, not a universal Reducto document limit. [Classify overview](https://docs.reducto.ai/classify/overview)

The response includes information that can help explain the category decision, including criterion-level details. That information is useful for diagnosing routing, but it should be interpreted within the content the operation was allowed to examine. [Classify response format](https://docs.reducto.ai/classify/response-format)

A fast document-level decision can be exactly what a well-defined intake workflow needs. The problem arises when the application expects that decision to describe every component of a mixed packet.

## When a file contains several documents

Reducto Split identifies page locations for described sections. Its documentation explicitly distinguishes section location from retrieval chunking. This allows downstream processing to target the relevant pages rather than assigning the whole file one processing contract. [Split documentation](https://docs.reducto.ai/split)

Use segmentation when an uploaded file can contain several invoices, a claim plus supporting records or statements for multiple accounts. The output needed by the application is then a map of components, not merely a category for the container.

A workflow may use classification and segmentation together. For example, classification can identify a packet family, after which segmentation separates the expected components. The important design choice is which question each operation answers and what happens when the packet does not match expectations.

## Work backward from the action after routing

Begin with the action that follows routing. If the entire file will use one extraction schema, a file-level label may be sufficient. If different pages require different schemas, section boundaries matter. If the same section type repeats for different people or accounts, entity grouping matters too.

| Intake requirement | Useful operation type |
| --- | --- |
| Route a single invoice | Whole-document classification |
| Find statements inside a bundle | Section segmentation |
| Separate several accounts' statements | Segmentation plus entity partitioning |
| Retrieve passages for a question | Content chunking and retrieval |
| Escalate uncertain or unsupported input | Explicit exception policy |

This table describes workflow requirements rather than promising that one endpoint resolves every task. It helps buyers avoid treating a higher-accuracy classification mode as a substitute for a different operation.

## The invoice on page 18

In this hypothetical 25-page insurance packet, the first five pages are a cover letter and administrative forms. A repair invoice appears on page 18, followed by photographs and a specialist report. No actual Reducto or LlamaIndex result is assumed.

If the workflow's question is “Which team should receive this claim packet?”, the first pages may be sufficient. If the question is “Does this packet contain a repair invoice?”, inspecting only the opening pages may omit decisive evidence. If the task is “Extract each invoice separately,” a file-level category cannot by itself provide invoice boundaries.

The correct design follows the required output. The application can segment the packet, identify components and route each component to its extraction schema. It should also record pages that remain unassigned so that unexpected material does not disappear from the workflow.

The example demonstrates a scope mismatch, not a product failure. Reducto's separate Split capability is precisely relevant to this kind of bundle.

## Make room for an uncertain route

Define an exception path before optimizing the happy path. A file may match multiple categories, match none or contain conflicting signals. The application needs a policy for such cases even when the API returns one best label.

Measure wrong-route consequences, not only classification accuracy. Sending an irrelevant file to an extractor may waste processing. Sending a document to a schema that omits important fields can create a more consequential silent error. Weight the review policy accordingly.

Keep category descriptions specific enough to distinguish neighboring types. Maintain examples of confusing pairs and review them when intake patterns change. This turns routing into an operationally maintained contract rather than a prompt written once and forgotten.

## A routing decision needs a defined scope

Compare the specified LlamaIndex workflow with the Reducto operation that matches the task. Name which pages each router sees, what it returns and how uncertainty is handled; the comparison should establish correct downstream records rather than reward the size of a vendor’s feature menu.

LlamaIndex publishes this guide. It describes product scope and workflow design; it does not report a measured routing comparison.

### Is Classify’s ten-page bound a parsing limit?

No. It applies to the selected PDF context for Classify. Treating it as a limit on Reducto’s entire platform would be incorrect.

### Does Deep Classify remove the need for Split?

The accurate classification mode still serves a classification task. If the application needs page boundaries or separate components, select an operation that produces them.

Start the intake trial with the documented LlamaParse Classify and Split APIs, then connect the selected source pages to schema-specific extraction. Measure wrong destinations, missed documents and accepted records against the corresponding vendor configuration. Keep Split’s beta status visible; no routing-accuracy superiority is established by the extraction benchmarks.

title: "Extend Operator-1 vs LlamaExtract Pricing: Accuracy per Dollar"

published: "2026-10-06"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/"
---

# Extend Operator-1 vs LlamaExtract Pricing: Accuracy per Dollar

In the pinned ExtractBench Pro snapshot, LlamaExtract Agentic Plus has higher Value F1 and more perfect documents than Extend Operator at a lower recorded cost per page. That is a measurable cost-and-quality reason to evaluate LlamaExtract first. Production costs still depend on the selected plan, effort, parsing, retries and the work needed to accept each document.

*Published by LlamaIndex. Prices describe the cited October 28 documentation snapshot, not a contractual quote or a new performance test.*

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on difficult documents

| Configuration | Value F1 | Perfect documents (%) | Recorded cost per 1,000 pages (\$) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 77.70 | 38.00 | 75.00 |
| Extend Operator | 73.87 | 34.00 | 98.80 |

Agentic Plus combines 77.70 Value F1 and 38% perfect documents with a recorded cost of \$75.00 per 1,000 pages. Extend Operator records 73.87, 34% and \$98.80 respectively. Those benchmark costs favor LlamaExtract in this snapshot; they are not a current contract quote or a measurement of production review time.

This is the pinned ExtractBench Pro snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026, with the 30-minute limit applied. Value results cover 100 synthetic long-tail documents; grounding uses an 81-document subset. Perfect documents means 100% Value F1 on the benchmark, not approval for an external business action. LlamaIndex publishes Pro and develops LlamaExtract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench-pro.md).

## What is included in the advertised extraction rate?

Extend documents Operator at five credits per page for extraction, with parsing separate. The base includes Operator-managed features; rare extra effort can add charges. Its credit documentation lists PAYG at \$0.01 per credit and Performance parsing at two credits per page. [Operator billing](https://docs.extend.ai/extraction/operator), [credit documentation](https://docs.extend.ai/general/how-credits-work).

Under those specific assumptions, Operator plus Performance parsing has a seven-cent-per-page base. That calculation excludes overages, other workflow actions and contractual discounts. It should not be presented as the cost of every Extend deployment.

List the stages you intend to buy before requesting a quote. A packet workflow may also need classification and splitting; an extraction-only quote will leave those costs out.

## How do you calculate cost per accepted document?

Use a denominator that reflects the business outcome:

**Cost per accepted document = total attributable processing and review cost ÷ documents satisfying the acceptance policy.**

Define acceptance before calculating the result. An accounts-payable team might require correct identifiers, complete line items and reconciled totals. A research ingestion team might accept a document if its text, tables and evidence support the intended retrieval tasks.

Keep cost categories visible rather than collapsing them immediately:

| Cost category | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Initial processing | Actual billed work for the first attempt |
| Retries and repairs | Additional attempts, changed settings and interventions |
| Human review | Review time using a stated labor-cost assumption |
| Downstream correction | Rework attributable to outputs accepted incorrectly |
| Infrastructure | Relevant orchestration, storage or customer-operated resources |

Keep the categories in the final report. They will show whether a higher processing bill bought fewer corrections, or whether simple forms passed just as reliably through a cheaper configuration.

## A 1,000-document budget example

Suppose a team processes 1,000 hypothetical documents with ten pages each. Applying the illustrative seven-cent base gives \$700 in initial processing charges. Assume, purely for explanation, another \$50 in retry charges and \$250 in review cost.

If 900 documents satisfy the acceptance policy, the resulting cost is \$1,000 divided by 900, or about \$1.11 per accepted document. Dividing the same spend by all 1,000 inputs would produce \$1.00, but would conceal the 100 inputs that did not reach the required outcome.

These are hypothetical inputs, not measured Extend or LlamaIndex results. Report the 100 unresolved documents beside the \$1.11 figure so the finance team can see the remaining work.

## Why should latency be measured alongside price?

A result delivered after the operational deadline may have less value than an equally accurate result delivered on time. Separate median latency from the tail, and separate a service's processing time from time spent waiting in your own queue.

Extend's synchronous endpoint has a five-minute limit; asynchronous processing follows a different execution pattern. That endpoint limit should not be confused with a benchmark's task budget. [Asynchronous processing documentation](https://docs.extend.ai/general/async-processing).

For a fair test, specify whether you measure upload-to-result, submission-to-result or processing-only time. Include queueing and retries if they affect the user experience. Report completion rate at the business deadline rather than silently excluding documents that take longer.

Use the same retry allowance for both vendors and include those retries in elapsed time.

## How should the document mix affect the budget?

Divide the evaluation corpus into useful operating groups: short forms, long tables, poor scans, dense diagrams and mixed document packets. Weight those groups by expected production volume, then retain the unweighted results so expensive exceptions remain visible.

Show the review bill for each group. A small set of difficult files can consume a disproportionate share of the budget.

Track changes over time as well. A customer rollout may begin with clean digital invoices and later add scans or unfamiliar suppliers. Reusing the original cost estimate without checking that shift can produce a budget miss even when product prices have not changed.

## When does Extend Operator make economic sense?

Operator can be a sensible candidate when agentic inspection and validation improve acceptance on difficult documents. Extend itself notes that Operator can be faster or cheaper than Performance for some large-table work, while difficult visual content can require more effort. [Operator operating guidance](https://docs.extend.ai/extraction/operator).

Compare LlamaIndex on the same document mix, acceptance policy and cost categories. Use published accuracy results to select candidates, then price the work your application needs.

## Ask for an itemized processing path

Start the cost-and-quality trial with the LlamaExtract configuration that leads the pinned Pro comparison. Reprice both products under current terms, then measure accepted documents, retries and review. The benchmark shows a lower recorded processing cost for Plus in that snapshot; it does not remove the need for a complete production budget.

title: "LlamaParse vs Datalab: What ParseBench Shows About Parsing Accuracy"
description: "LlamaParse Agentic Plus scores above Datalab Accurate on ParseBench, with particularly large differences in charts and visual grounding."
published: "2026-09-24"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/"
---

# LlamaParse vs Datalab: What ParseBench Shows About Parsing Accuracy

LlamaParse Agentic Plus scores above Datalab Accurate on ParseBench, with particularly large differences in charts and visual grounding. Those are relevant advantages for agents that must preserve numerical meaning and show evidence. OmniParseBench offers a different evaluation design; its scores should be read within that design rather than substituted for ParseBench results.

*Published by LlamaIndex, the organization behind ParseBench. This article reflects research through October 28, 2026 and acknowledges that publisher relationship explicitly.*

## Where LlamaParse performs better on ParseBench

| Configuration | Overall | Tables | Charts | Visual grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaParse Agentic Plus | 86.69 | 93.27 | 92.19 | 75.43 |
| Datalab Accurate | 72.88 | 90.66 | 63.20 | 51.38 |
| Datalab Balanced | 72.82 | 91.02 | 63.12 | 51.31 |

Agentic Plus leads Datalab Accurate by 13.81 points overall, 28.99 points on charts and 24.05 points on visual grounding. These are results on one named benchmark and its configurations; OmniParseBench uses different data and rules. The table supplies a concrete reason to evaluate LlamaParse without treating either benchmark as a universal verdict.

Scores are out of 100 in the pinned ParseBench snapshot (commit 0ccc167, November 2, 2026), checked for this revision on November 4. ParseBench measures document parsing across five dimensions, not schema extraction or the percentage of error-free documents. LlamaIndex develops LlamaParse and publishes this benchmark. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/blob/0ccc16783612a8ff37e77139f5e799510cde47b6/leaderboard.csv), [evaluation code and methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench).

## How does OmniParseBench add context to a LlamaParse decision?

OmniParseBench uses page-level tests grouped into text, tables and layout. Its overall result averages those family scores, and systems without layout output do not receive the same headline result. Its design also records information about test derivation and supports slicing by document characteristics. [OmniParseBench design](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench/blob/main/docs/design.md), [repository](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench).

Those choices make the output contract important. A system designed to return text alone may be useful for a specific application while not satisfying the benchmark’s full requirements. Conversely, returning the expected structure is necessary but does not guarantee that all downstream extraction tasks will work.

Benchmark results are most useful when a buyer can trace a score to individual examples. That makes it possible to distinguish a meaningful failure from an output difference the application can tolerate.

## Why rankings diverge

A benchmark defines a sample of work and a definition of success. Change either and the ranking can change without either experiment being fabricated.

| Design choice | Why it can change a ranking |
| --- | --- |
| Document mix | A multilingual scan workload differs from clean digital reports |
| Output contract | Text, chart data and visual grounding require different capabilities |
| Normalization | Equivalent representations may receive different treatment |
| Aggregation | Equal family weights differ from weighting every test equally |
| Failure policy | Excluding failed pages differs from counting them against completion |
| Configuration | Default and feature-enabled runs may request different outputs |

Check these choices before combining results. Averaging scores from incompatible experiments can obscure the very differences a buyer needs to understand.

## What should buyers make of Datalab’s ParseBench criticism?

Datalab has publicly challenged ParseBench’s formatting, chart-estimation and grounding methodology. Its critique includes a Surya research result on four non-chart dimensions and claims that configuration changes can substantially affect scores. The claims need to be checked against the cited configuration and scorer. [Datalab’s October 12 critique](https://www.datalab.to/blog/why-we-built-omniparsebench).

One important qualification concerns the cited Pulse configuration change. The associated ParseBench pull request describes fixing a refinement configuration issue as well as making requested formatting explicit. A gain following that change cannot simply be described as proof that identical outputs received a better score through normalization alone. [ParseBench pull request 121](https://github.com/run-llama/ParseBench/pull/121).

An adapter can change what a product is asked to do. Keep its revision with the result, and document corrections so readers can follow how a published score changed.

## Formatting that changes a document’s meaning

Formatting can carry meaning. A heading can define scope; a strike-through can indicate deletion; a table header can determine what a number represents. An application may legitimately need these features preserved.

At the same time, equivalent serializations should not be confused with different source meaning. If two representations preserve the same required semantics, an evaluation should explain why one would pass and the other fail.

Consider a hypothetical document in which a contract amendment strikes out an old payment date and inserts a new one. A plain-text output containing both dates may be inadequate for the application even if every character is recognized. The deleted-date markup is necessary to interpret the amendment.

Now consider two equivalent ways to encode emphasis in Markdown. If the application treats them identically, penalizing one may not reflect the buyer’s needs. These examples show why the rubric should state which distinctions matter.

## A case-level investigation

Select a small, representative group of disagreement cases. For each one, inspect the original page, the requested output, the raw response and the test verdict.

Classify the difference before assigning blame:

1. A genuine missing or incorrect fact.
2. A structural relationship the application needs.
3. An equivalent output representation.
4. An ambiguous reference or estimate.
5. A configuration mismatch.
6. A scoring or implementation issue requiring correction.

Keep the original scores while reporting any corrected analysis. Quietly changing a scorer or adapter makes it difficult to understand whether a new result reflects better parsing or a different experiment.

Also compare timing definitions. OmniParseBench’s results documentation explicitly distinguishes newer full-page timing from historical timing of successful unretried HTML calls. Those measurements should not be presented as directly comparable latency points. [Results methodology](https://github.com/datalab-to/omni_parse_bench/blob/main/docs/results.md).

## The private holdout still matters

Add a private holdout representing the actual workload. Keep its documents and scoring decisions separate from configuration tuning. Include failure cases with real operational consequences, not only visually impressive examples.

Use the public tests to locate likely risks, then check those risks on the holdout. In a LlamaIndex comparison, report the categories where a competitor performs better alongside the categories favoring our products.

Use LlamaParse’s measured ParseBench advantage to decide which configuration to trial first. Keep OmniParseBench and vendor criticisms as additional evidence about tasks and scoring, then verify the critical differences on a private holdout. State the benchmark and configuration beside each score.

title: "Reducto Deep Extract vs LlamaExtract: Long-Tail Accuracy and Missing Records"
description: "LlamaExtract Agentic Plus has higher Value F1 and many more perfect documents than Reducto Deep in the pinned ExtractBench Pro results."
published: "2026-09-18"
updated: "2026-11-04"
source: "https://developers.llamaindex.ai/"
---

# Reducto Deep Extract vs LlamaExtract: Long-Tail Accuracy and Missing Records

LlamaExtract Agentic Plus has higher Value F1 and many more perfect documents than Reducto Deep in the pinned ExtractBench Pro results. On standard ExtractBench, their overall value scores are much closer. That contrast matters for buyers whose expensive failures come from unusual documents, missing records and cross-page dependencies rather than ordinary forms.

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on ExtractBench

| Configuration | Value F1 | Long-document Value F1 | Word grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 96.17 | 94.65 | 83.25 |
| Reducto Deep Extract | 96.08 | 92.85 | 50.76 |

Standard ExtractBench Value F1 is close: 96.17 versus 96.08, only 0.09 points. That small average difference alone is a weak reason to choose a vendor; the grounding and long-tail results are more useful distinctions.

These are published results from the pinned ExtractBench snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026. The suite covers 370 documents and 4,869 pages. Value F1 measures extracted values; it is not a straight-through-processing rate. LlamaIndex publishes the benchmark and develops LlamaExtract, now documented within LlamaParse Extract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench.md).

## Where LlamaExtract performs better on difficult documents

| Configuration | Value F1 | Perfect documents (%) | Box-word grounding | Page grounding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| LlamaExtract Agentic Plus | 77.70 | 38.00 | 60.39 | 66.01 |
| Reducto Deep | 56.35 | 3.00 | 42.20 | 62.38 |

On Pro, Agentic Plus leads by 21.35 Value F1 points and 35 percentage points in perfect documents. That is a concrete long-tail advantage. It is not a measured missing-row recovery rate for the synthetic bank-statement fixture below.

This is the pinned ExtractBench Pro snapshot at commit 7004e29, checked on November 4, 2026, with the 30-minute limit applied. Value results cover 100 synthetic long-tail documents; grounding uses an 81-document subset. Perfect documents means 100% Value F1 on the benchmark, not approval for an external business action. LlamaIndex publishes Pro and develops LlamaExtract. [Pinned results](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/leaderboard-pro.csv), [methodology](https://github.com/run-llama/ExtractBench/blob/7004e297707163c492e5c449d89af3c708996f59/docs/extractbench-pro.md).

## The boundary of Deep Extract’s verification loop

Reducto Deep Extract uses an iterative verification process that can revise extracted output against instructions such as row counts and totals. Its documentation also identifies a boundary: the loop can verify only information available in the parsed representation. Information absent from Parse is outside that loop's view. This is a documented architectural constraint, not evidence that omissions occur frequently. [Deep Extract documentation](https://docs.reducto.ai/configs/extract/deep-extract)

The model versions must also be explicit. The reviewed registry identifies Deep Extract v3 as default and v4 as alpha, separately from standard Extract. Enabling Deep Extract overrides the standard extraction-model selection. A comparison should name the selected Deep Extract version rather than describing every extraction run as the same product. [Reducto model versions](https://docs.reducto.ai/reference/model-versions)

Inspect the handoff between the source pages, parsed content and extracted records. Looking only at the final JSON can leave the cause of an omission hidden.

## Where the expected total comes from matters

Reconciliation checks relationships among values. Its strength depends on where the expected relationship comes from. Summing extracted line items and comparing that sum with an independently verified source total is stronger than comparing two totals generated from the same incomplete record set.

A self-consistent output may still be incomplete if all of its checks share the same missing information. Conversely, a mismatch can be valuable: it tells the workflow to stop, investigate or request review. The objective should be reliable acceptance decisions, not forcing every document to produce a confident answer.

Design checks with independent evidence wherever possible. Source page counts, labeled record identifiers, externally supplied transaction counts and human-verified totals can each reveal a different class of omission.

## Build a source inventory

Use a labeled source inventory. Each required item needs a stable identifier, a source location and its expected output representation. For a statement, the inventory might include transactions, opening and closing balances, fees and continuation-page records.

| Measure | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Item recall | Did all required source records appear? |
| Field correctness | Are values correct within recovered records? |
| Duplicate handling | Were repeated records preserved or incorrectly added? |
| Evidence coverage | Can each accepted record be traced to the source? |
| Document acceptance | Did the workflow correctly accept or escalate the file? |

Keep document completion coverage separate. A system that declines a difficult statement should not receive the same interpretation as one that returns an incomplete statement without a warning. The former creates review work; the latter can let an incomplete record proceed.

## A synthetic five-row omission

In a synthetic test fixture, a six-page statement contains 120 transactions. A labeled fixture records all 120 transaction IDs. To demonstrate the evaluation method, deliberately remove a block of five transactions from an intermediate representation. This is a synthetic fault injection, not an observed Reducto or LlamaExtract failure.

An extractor operating on that altered representation may produce 115 well-formed records. Every amount it returns could be correct. A field-accuracy calculation over only those returned records could look excellent while the record inventory exposes the omission immediately.

Now add an independently verified closing balance and fee total. The workflow should check whether the extracted transactions reconcile to those source facts. If they do not, the correct result is an exception requiring investigation. If they happen to reconcile because offsetting entries were removed, the independent transaction inventory still detects the missing records.

Keep synthetic fault-injection results separate from runs on unmodified documents. Preserve raw outputs in both, so a deliberately removed block cannot be mistaken for a vendor error.

## Keep the test independent of prompt tuning

Use the same source documents, field definitions and acceptance rules. Give each system the information it would receive in production. If the schema includes an expected row count, disclose where that count came from and provide it consistently.

Include long tables, repeated transactions, continuation rows and irrelevant appendices. Choose them because they represent the workload, not because they were selected after one vendor failed. Freeze the test set before tuning prompts on a separate development set.

For each run, preserve the source, request, model configuration, raw output and validation report. Review omissions at the stage where they arise. A wrong final value may result from parsing, extraction, normalization or application logic; a useful report distinguishes these causes.

## Decide what happens when the checks disagree

Deep Extract already supports iterative checking and re-extraction on complex documents. The existence of a verification loop is therefore a poor basis for claiming that LlamaIndex is different. The useful comparison is what each workflow does when the records, totals and source coverage disagree.

A correct escalation can protect an application, but it still consumes review time. Report it separately from an incomplete output that was accepted without warning. The operating policy should explain which files proceed automatically, which receive another processing step and which go to a person.

Start the difficult-document trial with LlamaExtract Agentic Plus, whose Pro value accuracy and perfect-document rate provide the stronger long-tail evidence. Keep the near-tie on standard ExtractBench visible. Test the independently labeled missing-record fixtures separately before claiming recovery-rate superiority.
